question: H2
answer:
ANSWER

A driver of a commercial motor vehicle subject to the federal DOT/FMCSA drug and alcohol testing rules is barred from safety-sensitive duty at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater.

Regulatory text (49 CFR 382.201, 'Alcohol concentration'):

  'No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions.'

[66 FR 43103, Aug. 17, 2001, as amended at 77 FR 4483, Jan. 30, 2012]

1. UNIT — WHAT '0.04' IS MEASURED IN

49 CFR 382.107 defines the operative term: 'Alcohol concentration (or content) means the alcohol in a volume of breath expressed in terms of grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath as indicated by an evidential breath test under this part.'

So the regulatory quantity is breath alcohol concentration: 0.04 grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath. Because the definition fixes the breath measure to the standard blood/breath partition used in the rule, 0.04 g/210 L BrAC corresponds to 0.04 grams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood, i.e. 0.04% BAC. Both are the same threshold; 0.04 is not a different number in the two media.

2. THE PROHIBITION AND THE CONFIRMED VIOLATION USE THE SAME NUMBER

The two figures that are sometimes assumed to differ are the same under part 382:

- Pre-duty/on-duty prohibition (382.201): 0.04 or greater — do not report, do not remain on duty, and the employer must not permit performance.
- Confirmed violation triggering the return-to-duty process (382.217(b)): 'The driver receives an alcohol confirmation test result of 0.04 or higher alcohol concentration conducted under part 40 of this title.'

An employer may not allow, require, permit or authorize a driver to operate a CMV while the driver is not in compliance with the part 40 subpart O return-to-duty requirements after such a result.

3. BAND TABLE — SO THE BOUNDARIES ARE UNAMBIGUOUS

  Result (confirmation test)   Status under part 382
  ---------------------------  --------------------------------------------------------------
  Less than 0.02               Negative. No part 382 alcohol violation.
  0.02 or greater but          Not a violation of 382.201, but the driver must be removed from
  less than 0.04               safety-sensitive functions for 24 hours (part 40 alcohol testing
                               procedures; FMCSA part 382 guidance). No SAP/return-to-duty
                               process is triggered by this result alone.
  0.04 or greater              Violation. Driver is barred from safety-sensitive duty under
                               382.201; removal from safety-sensitive functions, SAP
                               evaluation, return-to-duty process under part 40 subpart O.

Return-to-duty threshold after a violation: the driver may not resume safety-sensitive functions until a return-to-duty alcohol test shows a concentration of less than 0.02 (see the part 382 return-to-duty provisions, e.g. 382.121's parallel non-DOT structure and part 40 subpart O), followed by follow-up testing.

4. PROHIBITIONS THAT DO NOT DEPEND ON A NUMBER

Part 382 subpart B bars certain conduct regardless of measured concentration, and these are commonly confused with the numeric threshold:

- 382.205 On-duty use: no driver may use alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions.
- 382.207 Pre-duty use: no driver may perform safety-sensitive functions within four hours after using alcohol. This is a time-based bar, not a concentration bar; a driver under 0.04 who drank within four hours is still prohibited.
- 382.209 Use following an accident (post-accident testing conduct rule).
- 382.211 Refusal to submit to a required test.

5. TESTING MECHANICS THAT AFFECT HOW THE THRESHOLD IS APPLIED

- A screening test result of 0.02 or greater requires an evidential breath confirmation test; the confirmation result is what establishes the concentration for purposes of 382.201 and 382.217(b).
- The regulatory measure is an evidential breath test result expressed in g/210 L. Alcohol concentration under part 382 is not established by urine testing, and blood testing is not the part 40 mechanism for DOT alcohol testing — the number is a breath number that is read as the blood-equivalent 0.04.
- The threshold is a 'or greater' floor: exactly 0.04 is a violation. There is no rounding allowance that permits a 0.04 driver to work.

6. SCOPE AND CAVEATS

- Modal scope: 49 CFR part 382 governs CDL drivers operating CMVs in interstate commerce. The other DOT modal administrations (FAA, FRA, FTA, PHMSA, USCG) each run their own alcohol rules under part 40 and likewise use 0.04 as the duty prohibition. If the requester needs a specific modal citation, part 382 is the one for CMV drivers.
- State law: state commercial driver alcohol limits can be stricter or differently structured, and state criminal per-se limits (commonly 0.08%) are a separate body of law that does not define the federal part 382 bar. The answer above is the federal threshold only.
- What this answer does not cover, because it was not asked: employer testing-program obligations (random rates, post-accident triggers), Clearinghouse reporting, SAP evaluation content, and follow-up testing schedules. Each is a separate question.

7. ONE-LINE ANSWER

0.04 or greater alcohol concentration — 0.04 grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (BrAC), equivalent to 0.04 g/100 mL blood (0.04% BAC) — under 49 CFR 382.201.

question: H4
answer:
Statutory answer for Great Britain (England and Wales and Scotland) under the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), as amended:

1. Paid annual leave: 5.6 weeks per leave year. This is the aggregate of 4 weeks under reg 13(1) and 1.6 weeks of additional leave under reg 13A(2)(e), which applies to leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2009. It is the statutory minimum, not contractual enhanced leave. Bank and public holidays may be included within it.

2. Cap: 28 days. Reg 13A(3) provides that the aggregate entitlement under reg 13(1) and reg 13A is subject to a maximum of 28 days. The cap is a cap on statutory entitlement, not a limit on what an employer may offer contractually. It applies regardless of the number of days a worker works each week: where the normal working week is longer than 5 days, the 5.6-week calculation is cut down to 28 days.

Conversion to days for a full leave year: statutory entitlement in days is the lower of 28 days and 5.6 x the number of days normally worked per week. Examples: a 5-day week gives 5.6 x 5 = 28 days, exactly at the cap; a 6-day week gives 5.6 x 6 = 33.6 days, capped at 28 days; a 4-day week gives 22.4 days; a 3-day week gives 16.8 days. Part-time and part-year workers are prorated. For irregular-hours and part-year workers from 1 April 2024, the separate accrual regime applies at 12.07% of hours worked, subject to the 28-day cap; that is the same 5.6-week entitlement expressed as an accrual method. Northern Ireland is outside the GB scope of this answer and has separate implementing regulations.

Therefore: ask 1 = 5.6 weeks; ask 2 = 28 days.

answer:
# DNS name size limits, per the original specification (RFC 1035 / RFC 1034, November 1987)

## 1. Answer

| Object | Limit | Unit | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| A single label | **63** | octets of label content | 6-bit length field in the label wire format |
| A full domain name | **255** | octets of wire format, *including* one length octet per label and the root's terminating zero octet | RFC 1035 §2.3.4 and §3.1 |
| (corollary) A full domain name in presentation/text form | **253** | characters, excluding the trailing dot (254 with it) | 255 − 2, derived below |
| Root name `.` | 1 | octet of wire format (a single zero length octet) | RFC 1035 §3.1 |

The 255-octet figure is a **wire-format** figure in the original specification itself; it is not a content-only figure. The frequently quoted 253 is the same limit expressed in the presentation format (the text form with dots), not a competing definition of the name limit.

## 2. Primary text (verbatim)

RFC 1035 §2.3.4, *Size limits*:

> labels          63 octets or less
> names           255 octets or less
> TTL             positive values of a signed 32 bit number.
> UDP messages    512 octets or less

RFC 1035 §3.1, *Name space definitions*:

> Each label is represented as a one octet length field followed by that number of octets. Since every domain name ends with the null label of the root, a domain name is terminated by a length byte of zero. The high order two bits of every length octet must be zero, and the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less.
>
> To simplify implementations, the total length of a domain name (i.e., label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less.

RFC 1034 §3.1, *Name space definitions*:

> Each node has a label, which is zero to 63 octets in length. ... One label is reserved, and that is the null (i.e., zero length) label used for the root.
>
> To simplify implementations, the total number of octets that represent a domain name (i.e., the sum of all label octets and label lengths) is limited to 255.

RFC 1035 §4.1.4 confirms the mechanism that forces 63 rather than 255:

> The first two bits are ones. This allows a pointer to be distinguished from a label, since the label must begin with two zero bits because labels are restricted to 63 octets or less.

Later clarifications restate, and do not change, the numbers:

- RFC 2181 §11: "The length of any one label is limited to between 1 and 63 octets. A full domain name is limited to 255 octets (including the separators). The zero length full name is defined as representing the root of the DNS tree..."
- RFC 9499 §2: "The length of each label is between 0 and 63 octets inclusive. In a fully qualified domain name, the last label in the ordered list is 0 octets long... A domain name in the global DNS has a maximum total length of 255 octets in the wire format; the root represents one octet for this calculation."

RFC 1123 relaxed only the *character-set* rules inherited from HOSTS.TXT (leading digit allowed); it did not alter either length limit. RFC 2181 §11's parenthetical "(including the separators)" is loose wording: in wire format there are no dot separators, and the octets actually counted are the length octets. Reading it as "255 characters of dotted text" would yield a 257-octet wire name and is wrong.

## 3. Derivation of each number

### 3.1 Label = 63

A label on the wire is `[LLLLLLLL][content...]`. The top two bits of the length octet must be `00` (they are `11` in a compression pointer, `01`/`10` reserved). That leaves 6 bits: `0b00111111` = 63. So the representable content length is 0..63, and 63 is the maximum.

### 3.2 Name = 255 (wire format)

For a name with `n` non-root labels of content lengths `L1..Ln`, terminated by the root:

```
wire_length = SUM(len(Li) + 1)  +  1
            = SUM(len(Li)) + n + 1      <= 255
```

The `+1` inside the sum is each label's length octet; the trailing `+1` is the root's zero length octet. Therefore the maximum content is `255 - n - 1 = 254 - n`, capped at `63n`:

```
max_content(n) = min(63 * n, 254 - n)
```

| n (labels) | 63n | 254−n | max content octets | max wire octets | max presentation chars |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 63 | 253 | 63 | 65 | 63 |
| 2 | 126 | 252 | 126 | 129 | 127 |
| 3 | 189 | 251 | 189 | 193 | 191 |
| 4 | 252 | 250 | **250** | **255** | **253** |
| 5 | 315 | 249 | 249 | 255 | 253 |
| 127 | 8001 | 127 | 127 | 255 | 253 |

The global maximum content (250 octets) occurs at n = 4: `63.63.63.61`. That is the longest legal name. Note that `63.63.63.63` (four maximal labels) is **illegal**: 252 + 4 + 1 = 257 octets, which exceeds 255.

### 3.3 The 253 figure (presentation form)

```
presentation_length = SUM(len(Li)) + (n - 1)      # dots between labels, no trailing dot
wire_length - presentation_length = (SUM + n + 1) - (SUM + n - 1) = 2
```

So for every name, presentation length = wire length − 2, and the maximum is 253 characters (254 if the trailing root dot is printed). This is where 253 comes from. It is not "255 minus the label length octets" in general — the difference is always exactly 2 (the first label's length octet and the root's terminator), regardless of how many labels there are.

## 4. What does and does not count toward 255

| Counts | Does not count |
|---|---|
| Every octet of every label's content | Dot separators (presentation only; not on the wire) |
| One length octet per label, including the root's zero octet | Compression pointers (2 octets in the message, but the name's 255 limit is on the *uncompressed* name) |
| — | Any per-RR or per-message framing (owner-name offset, TYPE/CLASS/TTL/RDLENGTH) |

A name is legal only if its **expanded** form fits in 255 octets. A compression pointer substitutes for the *encoding* of a suffix, not for its length. The 255 limit is a property of the name, not of the transport; the 512-octet UDP limit in the same RFC 1035 §2.3.4 table is a separate, unrelated constraint.

Edge cases:
- The root `.` is the *minimum* name (1 octet), not the maximum-length case. It is encoded as the single octet `0x00`.
- A zero-length label is legal only as the root (RFC 2181 §11: label length "between 1 and 63"; RFC 9499 §2: "it is the only label whose length may be 0 octets"). An empty interior label is malformed.
- Multicast DNS (RFC 6762) deliberately uses a different accounting (255 octets of content plus a terminator); RFC 9499 §2 calls this out explicitly. Do not mix the two when validating unicast DNS.

## 5. Reference implementation (application-layer validation)

```python
MAX_LABEL_OCTETS     = 63     # RFC 1035 3.1: 6-bit length field, high 2 bits reserved
MAX_NAME_WIRE_OCTETS = 255    # RFC 1035 3.1: label octets + label length octets, root included
MAX_NAME_PRES_OCTETS = 253    # corollary: 255 - 2 (first length octet + root terminator)

class NameTooLong(ValueError):
    pass

def wire_length(labels):
    """labels: list[bytes] of non-root labels, in order. Root is implicit."""
    return sum(len(l) + 1 for l in labels) + 1        # +1 per length octet, +1 for root

def presentation_length(labels):
    return sum(len(l) for l in labels) + max(len(labels) - 1, 0)

def validate_labels(labels):
    for i, lab in enumerate(labels):
        if len(lab) == 0:
            raise NameTooLong(f"empty label at index {i}: only the root may be zero-length")
        if len(lab) > MAX_LABEL_OCTETS:
            raise NameTooLong(f"label {i} is {len(lab)} octets; limit is {MAX_LABEL_OCTETS}")
    w = wire_length(labels)
    if w > MAX_NAME_WIRE_OCTETS:
        raise NameTooLong(f"name is {w} wire octets; limit is {MAX_NAME_WIRE_OCTETS}")
    return w

def encode_name(labels):
    """Uncompressed wire encoding. Caller is responsible for compression."""
    validate_labels(labels)
    out = bytearray()
    for lab in labels:
        out.append(len(lab))            # top two bits are zero by construction
        out += lab
    out.append(0)                       # root
    return bytes(out)

def decode_name(buf, offset, max_name_octets=MAX_NAME_WIRE_OCTETS):
    """Decompressing parser with an explicit expansion budget (anti-DoS)."""
    labels, pos, consumed, hops = [], offset, 0, 0
    while True:
        if pos >= len(buf):
            raise NameTooLong("truncated name")
        b = buf[pos]
        if b & 0xC0 == 0xC0:                       # 11xxxxxx: compression pointer
            if pos + 1 >= len(buf):
                raise NameTooLong("truncated pointer")
            if hops > 127:
                raise NameTooLong("pointer loop")
            target = ((b & 0x3F) << 8) | buf[pos + 1]
            if target >= pos:                      # only backward pointers are legal
                raise NameTooLong("forward compression pointer")
            if consumed == 0:
                consumed = pos + 2 - offset        # bytes used in the original stream
            pos = target
            hops += 1
            continue
        if b & 0xC0:                               # 01/10 reserved
            raise NameTooLong(f"reserved label type 0b{b >> 6:02b}")
        pos += 1
        if b == 0:                                 # root
            break
        if b > MAX_LABEL_OCTETS:
            raise NameTooLong(f"label length {b} exceeds {MAX_LABEL_OCTETS}")
        if pos + b > len(buf):
            raise NameTooLong("truncated label")
        labels.append(buf[pos:pos + b])
        pos += b
        if consumed == 0:
            consumed = pos - offset
    expanded = wire_length(labels)
    if expanded > max_name_octets:
        raise NameTooLong(f"expanded name is {expanded} octets; limit is {max_name_octets}")
    return labels, offset + (consumed if consumed else 1)
```

Notes on the parser: the budget is applied to the **expanded** length, never to the number of bytes consumed in the message; `consumed` tracks how far the caller should advance, which is a different number once a pointer is followed.

## 6. Acceptance test vectors

| Case | Labels | Wire octets | Presentation chars | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Root | (none) | 1 | 0 | accept |
| Single max label | 63 | 65 | 63 | accept |
| Label of 64 | 64 | — | — | reject (label limit) |
| Interior empty label | `a`, ``, `b` | — | — | reject (zero-length non-root) |
| Longest legal name | 63.63.63.61 | 255 | 253 | accept (both bounds exact) |
| One octet too long | 63.63.63.62 | 256 | 254 | reject (name limit) |
| Four maximal labels | 63.63.63.63 | 257 | 255 | reject (name limit) |
| Many short labels | 127 × 1-octet | 255 | 253 | accept (both bounds exact) |
| 128 × 1-octet | 128 × 1-octet | 257 | 255 | reject (name limit) |
| Compressed suffix | pointer to a 63-octet label | 2 in message, 65 expanded | 63 | accept; limit applies to the 65, not the 2 |

## 7. Implementation checklist (traps to avoid)

1. Do not enforce 255 against the compressed byte count — enforce it against the expanded name, or a compression bomb bypasses the check.
2. Do not enforce 255 as content-only. RFC 1035 §3.1 counts "label octets and label length octets"; content-only 255 would permit a 257-octet wire name.
3. Do not enforce 253 on the wire. 253 is a presentation-form figure; applying it to wire bytes rejects the legal `63.63.63.61` name.
4. Count the root's zero octet exactly once. Off-by-one here produces the classic 255-vs-256 disagreement.
5. Apply the same checks to names embedded in RDATA (SOA MNAME/RNAME, NS, MX, PTR, CNAME, SRV), not just to QNAME/owner names.
6. When generating, reject before encoding; when parsing, reject after expansion. Two different code paths, one shared `validate_labels`.
7. Do not conflate the 255-octet name limit with the 512-octet UDP message limit from the same RFC 1035 §2.3.4 table, nor with the 255-octet content accounting used by mDNS (RFC 6762).

## 8. Summary of the answer as stated

- **Label: 63 octets maximum** (0..63 representable; 0 only for the root).
- **Full name: 255 octets maximum on the wire**, counting all label content plus one length octet per label plus the root's terminating zero octet; equivalently **253 characters maximum in presentation form** excluding the trailing dot (254 including it).
- Longest legal name: `63.63.63.61` = 250 octets of content = 255 wire octets = 253 presentation characters.

question: H8
answer:
US FEDERAL MCL FOR PFOA IN DRINKING WATER

1. THE VALUE AND ITS SOURCE

The federal maximum contaminant level (MCL) for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is set in 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart G, Sec. 141.61(c)(2) ("MCLs and HBWCs for PFAS"), Table row (vi), promulgated in the PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (89 FR 32532, Apr. 26, 2024).

2. AS THE RULE LISTS IT (ask 2)

The table columns are: CAS. No. | Contaminant | MCL (mg/l) (unless otherwise noted) | HBWC (mg/l) for Hazard Index calculation.

The PFOA row reads, verbatim:

  (vi)  45285-51-6  |  PFOA  |  0.0000040  |  Not applicable.

So the rule lists the PFOA MCL as 0.0000040 mg/l (4.0 x 10^-6 mg/L), with the trailing zero retained because that is how the codified text is printed (two significant figures). Note the unit is the table's default, milligrams per litre, not the ppt figure EPA uses in outreach materials.

3. IN NANOGRAMS PER LITRE (ask 3)

Exact unit conversion, no rounding:

  0.0000040 mg/L x (1,000 ug / 1 mg) = 0.0040 ug/L
  0.0040 ug/L x (1,000 ng / 1 ug) = 4.0 ng/L

Equivalently: 0.0000040 mg/L x (1,000,000 ng / 1 mg) = 4.0 ng/L.

  PFOA MCL = 4.0 ng/L (= 4.0 nanograms per litre = 4.0 parts per trillion = 0.0040 ug/L = 0.0000040 mg/L)

This agrees with EPA's own listing on its PFAS NPDWR page: "PFOA ... 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)," and with EPA's technical overview: "EPA is setting enforceable Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) at 4.0 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS, individually." The Part 141 key defines "ppt = parts per trillion, or nanograms per liter."

4. VALUES THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH THE MCL (stated so the reader can check the arithmetic above against them)

- MCLG for PFOA: 0 (zero). Non-enforceable health goal; the enforceable MCL is 4.0 ng/L. Not a substitute for the MCL.
- PFOS MCL: also 0.0000040 mg/l (4.0 ng/L), a separate individual MCL, not a combined PFOA+PFOS total. The rule does not set a combined PFOA+PFOS MCL; it sets five individual MCLs (PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA) plus a unitless Hazard Index MCL of 1 for mixtures of two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS. PFOA is not a Hazard Index component (its HBWC cell reads "Not applicable").
- Trigger level for PFOA under Sec. 141.902(a)(5): 2.0 ng/L. This is a monitoring/reporting trigger, deliberately below the MCL; it is NOT the MCL and does not modify the 4.0 ng/L value.
- PQL for PFOA: 4.0 ppt, i.e., the MCL is set at the practical quantitation level.

5. STATUS / EFFECTIVE DATE CAVEAT

Sec. 141.60(a)(4) states: "The effective date for Sec. 141.61(c)(2)(i) through (vii) is April 26, 2029." The codified text above is therefore the promulgated federal MCL, with a 2029 effective/compliance date; EPA's implementation timeline is initial monitoring by 2027 and treatment installed by 2029. This rule has been the subject of litigation and administrative reconsideration proposals, so before relying on the figure for a compliance determination, re-verify Sec. 141.61(c)(2)(vi) at eCFR (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-141/subpart-G) and check for any stay, amendment, or remand affecting the PFOA row. The value stated here reflects the eCFR text as fetched 2026-11-17.

6. ANSWER IN ONE LINE

PFOA MCL: 0.0000040 mg/l as listed in 40 CFR 141.61(c)(2)(vi) - equal to 4.0 ng/L (4.0 ppt).

Confirm against the printed Rev. Z PDF (SNVS774Z) before releasing the number into a controlled document.

DESIGN USE (why these two numbers matter on a board)

Reference voltage sets output accuracy. Standard LM317 transfer function:
  V_O = V_REF · (1 + R2/R1) + I_ADJ · R2, with V_REF = 1.25 V typ and I_ADJ ≈ 50 µA typ.
  With R1 = 240 Ω (the datasheet's customary value, chosen to keep I_ADJ negligible and satisfy minimum load), R2 = 720 Ω gives V_O ≈ 1.25 · (1 + 3) = 5.00 V nominal.
  Worst-case tolerance from V_REF alone over temperature: 1.20/1.25 → −4.0%, 1.30/1.25 → +4.0%, i.e. 4.80 V to 5.20 V at the 5 V setpoint before resistor tolerance. Budget this explicitly; if ±1% output is required, the LM317A (tighter V_REF window, per its own datasheet — do not blend LM317A limits into a standard LM317 budget) or a different topology is needed. Use 1% or better resistors for R1/R2, since resistor ratio error adds directly to the V_REF error.

Differential limit drives topology and protection.
  - The regulator is floating: it senses only V_I − V_O, so the input may sit at a high voltage above ground provided the 40 V differential is never exceeded. The ADJ pin and the resistor divider must therefore be rated for the full input-to-ground voltage, and the divider's lower resistor must not be allowed to see a ground-referenced fault that exceeds the differential.
  - Keep steady-state V_I − V_O well below 40 V; the excess is dissipated as heat: P = (V_I − V_O) · I_O. At 1.5 A, even 10 V differential is 15 W — a TO-220 standing in still air cannot do this without a heatsink; this is usually the real binding constraint, not the 40 V stress rating.
  - Reverse-differential hazard: if the input is shorted or crowbarred to ground while a large output capacitor holds charge, V_O − V_I goes positive and the 40 V differential can be exceeded in reverse, damaging the device. Add a reverse-protection diode from OUTPUT (anode) to INPUT (cathode) whenever C_O > 10 µF, and a similar diode from OUTPUT to ADJ when an ADJ bypass capacitor is used, so those capacitors discharge through the diode rather than through the device junctions.
  - Output short circuit is a normal, specified condition for the LM317 (current limiting and thermal shutdown are internal), but the short-circuit path still must not exceed the 40 V differential; a shorted output with a high input rail is exactly the case that breaches it — verify the input rail plus any transient overshoot stays ≤ 40 V across the device under the short condition.

UNIT AND PRECISION CONVENTION
Reported in volts, as printed: 40 V (two significant figures, exact as a rating) and 1.25 V (three significant figures, as printed in the typ column). # Minimum rest between duty days for a US airline flight attendant

## Bottom line

**10 consecutive hours.** Under 14 CFR §121.467(b)(2), a flight attendant on a scheduled duty period of **14 hours or less** must be given a scheduled rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours**, and under (b)(3) that 10 hours **may not be reduced**. Ten consecutive hours is therefore both the base-case requirement and the absolute regulatory floor for Part 121 flight attendants.

One qualifier changes the number, not the floor: if the flight attendant is scheduled to a duty period of **more than 14 hours but not more than 20 hours**, the required rest rises to **12 consecutive hours** (b)(7), reducible back to 10 only if a **subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours** begins no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest (b)(8).

So: **10 hours is the answer; 12 hours applies to extended duty days.**

## Controlling rule and scope

- Citation: 14 CFR §121.467, "Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: Domestic, flag, and supplemental operations."
- Applies to certificate holders conducting **domestic, flag, or supplemental** operations under Part 121 — i.e., scheduled US airlines and their cabin crew.
- The rest period "must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period" (b)(2), (b)(7). It is measured duty-end to next-duty-start, not airport-to-hotel.
- Part 117 (the 10-hour/8-hour flight-time regime the public usually associates with "pilot rest") applies to **flightcrew members**, not flight attendants. It is not the authority for cabin crew. The flight-attendant rules sit in Part 121 Subpart P.
- If the operation is **Part 135**, §121.467 does not apply by its terms. No equivalent FAA flight-attendant rest minimum appears in the grounded sources for Part 135; that would require separate research before any number is quoted.

## Rest required, by scheduled duty period length

| Scheduled duty period | Required scheduled rest | Reducible? | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less | **10 consecutive hours** | **No** — may not be reduced below 10 | §121.467(b)(1)–(b)(3) |
| More than 14, up to 16 hours (requires at least one flight attendant above the minimum complement) | 12 consecutive hours | Yes, to 10, with 14h compensatory rest | §121.467(b)(4), (b)(7), (b)(8) |
| More than 16, up to 20 hours (requires additional flight attendants above the minimum complement — three additional in the longest tier) | 12 consecutive hours | Yes, to 10, with 14h compensatory rest | §121.467(b)(5), (b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(8) |

Note on the extended tiers: the excerpts captured (b)(4) in full (14–16 hours, one additional flight attendant above the operations-specification minimum) and only the tail of (b)(6) ("at least three flight attendants in addition to the minimum flight attendant complement"). The exact staffing condition in (b)(5) and the exact ceiling in (b)(6) should be read off the current eCFR text before being used to build a pairing. They do not change the 10/12-hour rest answer.

## How the 12-to-10 reduction works

For a duty period over 14 hours, the 12-hour rest may be "scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours" **only if** the flight attendant is provided a **subsequent rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours** that:

1. is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**, and
2. occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

§121.467(b)(8). In practice: reduce tonight to 10, and tomorrow's rest must be 14 or more and must start within 24 hours of the start of tonight's 10. The reduction is not free — it is a loan repaid within one day.

There is no equivalent reduction available in the 14-hours-or-less tier. Ten is a hard floor there.

## What does and does not count as rest

- **No duty during rest.** "No certificate holder ... may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period." §121.467(b)(11).
- **Company-required non-local transportation is not rest.** Time spent in transportation, not local in character, that the carrier requires and provides to move the flight attendant to an airport to serve a flight, or from the airport where relieved back to home station, is excluded from the rest period. §121.467(b)(12). Practically, a long deadhead or a required van ride does not stop the rest clock from running only because the flight attendant is sitting down — it is carved out of rest, so the rest window must be sized around it.
- **Actual rest, not just paper rest.** The rule text also bars assigning a flight attendant to any duty period "unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section" (partial text at (b)(10) in the source excerpt). A schedule that nominally allows 10 hours but is eaten by an arrival delay does not satisfy the rule. Confirm the exact wording of (b)(10) against eCFR before relying on it in a delay dispute.

## Separate requirement that is often confused with this one

**24 consecutive hours free from all duty in any 7 consecutive calendar days.** §121.467(b)(13). This is a weekly relief requirement, not the between-duty-days rest period. It does not substitute for, and is not satisfied by, the 10- or 12-hour rest. Keep the two in separate lines of a compliance check.

## Layers above the federal minimum

- **Collective bargaining agreements.** The FAA minimum is a floor. Cabin crew CBAs routinely provide 11–12 hours of rest on all duty days, hotel-minimum and duty-rig provisions, and restrictions on reduced rest. A carrier's actual obligation to a given flight attendant is the greater of the regulation and the CBA. If the question is "what must *this* airline give *this* flight attendant," the CBA governs once it exceeds 10/12.
- **State and local meal/rest-break law.** A 2026 NPRM would add §121.468 providing that §121.467 preempts state and local law, rule, regulation, order, or standard covering flight attendant duty and rest periods, including meal and rest breaks (and a parallel §117.31 for flightcrew). As of the source, this is a **proposed** rule, not final. Until it is final and effective, do not assume state break law is preempted; California-style break rules remain a live question for carriers with crew based there. Verify current Federal Register status before advising.
- **Part 91K fractional program managers.** §91.1062 imposes a different scheme — 9 consecutive hours for duty of 14 hours or less, reducible to 8 with a 10-hour compensatory rest, and 12 hours for extended duty. This is **not** the airline answer; it is included only so the 9/8 figures are not mistaken for a Part 121 requirement.

## Worked check

Scheduled duty ends 21:00 after a 12-hour 30-minute duty day.

- Duty length 12:30 ≤ 14:00 → 10-hour tier.
- 10 hours cannot be reduced → earliest next duty commencement is **07:00 the following day**.
- If the carrier had scheduled a 15-hour 30-minute duty day ending at 21:00, the rest would be 12 hours → earliest next duty 09:00, unless the carrier elected the (b)(8) reduction to 10 (earliest 07:00), in which case the next rest must be ≥14 hours and must begin no later than 24 hours after 07:00 — i.e., by 07:00 the following morning.

## Compliance verification steps

1. Classify the operation: Part 121 domestic, flag, or supplemental. If Part 135, stop — this rule does not apply.
2. Determine the **scheduled** duty period length for the day just worked.
3. ≤14:00 → require ≥10 consecutive hours, no reduction permitted.
4. >14:00 and ≤20:00 → require ≥12 consecutive hours; check that the extended-duty staffing condition in (b)(4)–(b)(6) was actually satisfied, or the duty period itself was illegal.
5. If 12 was reduced to 10, verify the 14-hour compensatory rest is scheduled and begins within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest.
6. Exclude company-required non-local transportation from the rest window; confirm the resulting actual rest still meets the minimum after any arrival delay.
7. Confirm no duty was assigned during the rest period.
8. Separately confirm the 24-in-7 relief.
9. Overlay the CBA and any non-preempted state requirement; the binding number is the highest applicable.

## Caveats

- Figures are the federal regulatory minimum for Part 121 flight attendants. They are not a statement of any particular airline's contractual obligation.
- The §121.468 preemption provision and the parallel §117.31 are from a 2026 notice of proposed rulemaking; they are not final. Do not cite them as operative law.
- Paragraphs (b)(5), (b)(6) and (b)(9)–(b)(10) of §121.467 were only partially captured in the source excerpts; confirm their exact text at eCFR before relying on the extended-duty staffing thresholds or the actual-rest prohibition in an enforcement context. The 10-hour and 12-hour rest values themselves are confirmed by multiple independent renderings of §121.467(b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(7) and (b)(8).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-121/subpart-p/subject-group-ecfrb49759e744c709b/section-121.467 and 9 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.1062. The first reads: "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."

question: H3
answer:
ANSWER

Under the FAA rules, a drone counts as a "small unmanned aircraft" (the regulatory term behind "small drone") only if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS on takeoff, including everything on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft. That is 24.9476 kg (FAA commonly rounds this to 25 kg). The limit is exclusive: a drone at exactly 55.00 lb is not a small UAS. There is therefore no single heaviest qualifying weight; any takeoff weight strictly below 55 lb qualifies (e.g., 54.99 lb), and 55.00 lb or more does not.

REGULATORY BASIS

1. 14 CFR 107.3 (definitions): "Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft." This is the controlling definition for Part 107.
2. FAA, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Regulations (Part 107): "The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) rules for small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), or 'drone,' operations cover a broad spectrum of commercial and government uses for drones weighing less than 55 pounds." The same page's rule summary states: "Unmanned aircraft must weigh less than 55 lbs. (25 kg)."
3. FAA Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) 11-1-1: "part 107 operations are limited to small UAS (sUAS) weighing less than 55 pounds."
4. AIM 11-1-2: "Generally, UAS weighing less than 55 pounds MGOW are permitted to operate within Visual Line of Sight (VLOS) up to 400 feet Above Ground Level (AGL) in uncontrolled (Class G) airspace." MGOW = maximum gross operating weight.
5. AIM 11-1-2: "Public UAS, and civil UAS 55 pounds or more MGOW operate under 14 CFR part 91, UAS operations." So 55 lb or more is the large-UAS side of the line.

WHAT THE WEIGHT INCLUDES

- Total weight of the unmanned aircraft at takeoff: airframe, motors, propellers, batteries, attached cameras/sensors, payload, cargo, and anything else on board or attached. Not empty weight.
- Part 107 summary on carriage of property for compensation or hire: "The aircraft, including its attached systems, payload and cargo weigh less than 55 pounds total."
- The ground control station / transmitter is not part of the aircraft and does not count toward the 55 lb.
- Practical consequence: adding a payload can push a compliant aircraft over the line; the aircraft must be under 55 lb as configured for that flight, at takeoff.

EDGE CASES AND RELATED THRESHOLDS (do not confuse them)

| Takeoff weight (all-up, as flown) | Small UAS? | Governing regime |
|---|---|---|
| 0.55 lb (250 g) or less | Yes | Part 107 applies; also eligible for Category 1 operations over people if it has no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate skin |
| More than 0.55 lb but less than 55 lb | Yes | Part 107; registration required for all Part 107 operations regardless of weight |
| Exactly 55.00 lb | No | 55 lb or more MGOW = large UAS; Part 91 UAS operations with a COA, experimental certificate under 14 CFR 21.191, and Part 47 N-number registration |
| More than 55 lb | No | Same large-UAS path |

- 0.55 lb (250 g) is NOT the small-drone ceiling. It is (a) the Category 1 operations-over-people weight limit and (b) the weight above which a purely recreational UAS must be registered. It is far below the 55 lb small-UAS definition.
- Registration thresholds: all Part 107 UAS must be registered regardless of weight; recreational UAS must be registered if over 0.55 lb (250 g); UAS under 55 lb may use the Part 48 online system, while UAS at 55 lb MGOW or more must be registered under Part 47 (N-number).
- Part 107's operations-over-people Categories 2 and 3 are eligibility/kinetic-energy based rather than a fixed weight ceiling, but every aircraft used under Part 107 must still satisfy the less-than-55-lb small UAS definition.

WHAT HAPPENS ABOVE 55 LB

Exceeding 55 lb does not make flight illegal; it moves the operation outside Part 107. The operator needs a different authority — typically 14 CFR Part 91 UAS operations with a Certificate of Authorization (COA) or waiver, an experimental airworthiness certificate under 14 CFR 21.191, and Part 47 registration. Part 107 waivers do not convert a 55 lb-or-more aircraft into a small UAS; the weight limit is part of the rule's applicability, not a waivable operating limitation.

METRIC CONVERSION AND A TRAP

- 55 lb × 0.45359237 kg/lb = 24.94758035 kg. The true metric bound is therefore less than 24.9476 kg (about 24.95 kg).
- The FAA's rounded "25 kg" is shorthand only. 25.00 kg = 55.1156 lb, which is above 55 lb. Do not use 25 kg as an inclusive ceiling: a 25.00 kg aircraft is not a small UAS. For compliance work, use 24.9476 kg or 24.95 kg.

CURRENCY

Based on the current eCFR text of 14 CFR Part 107 and FAA Part 107/AIM pages as fetched 2026-11-17. The less-than-55-lb definition has been stable since Part 107 took effect in 2016; the 2021 operations-over-people rule added Categories 1–4 without changing the 55 lb small-UAS definition. Re-verify before relying on it for a specific operation, since thresholds and categories can be amended.

BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL (FAA, 14 CFR 91.155)

JURISDICTION / SOURCE
Answered under U.S. FAA rules, 14 CFR §91.155 'Basic VFR weather minimums' (paragraph (a) table), as reproduced in FAA AIM 3-1-4 / TBL 3-1-1. Verified against eCFR, the FAA's 91.155 PDF, the govinfo CFR-2026-title14-vol2 text, and AIM Chapter 3 Section 1 — all four agree. If a non-U.S. regulatory framework is intended, these numbers do not apply; the request does not name a jurisdiction, and FAR Part 91 is the standard framing of this question.

THE ANSWER (Class E, less than 10,000 ft MSL)

  Flight visibility ....... 3 statute miles
  Distance from clouds .... 500 feet below the cloud
                            1,000 feet above the cloud
                            2,000 feet horizontal from the cloud

All three cloud clearances apply simultaneously — the aircraft must satisfy the below, above, and horizontal distances at once, not any one of them.

REGULATORY TEXT (§91.155(a), Class E row)
  'Class E:
   Less than 10,000 feet MSL ....... 3 statute miles .... 500 feet below.
                                                          1,000 feet above.
                                                          2,000 feet horizontal.'

BOUNDARIES AND WHAT THEY MEAN
- 'Less than 10,000 ft MSL' is exclusive: at exactly 10,000 ft MSL and above, the Class E minimums change to 5 statute miles visibility, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, and 1 statute mile horizontal. Do not apply the 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 set at or above 10,000 MSL.
- Class E below 10,000 ft MSL is not split by day/night and not split at 1,200 ft AGL for the basic VFR cloud-clearance rule. The day/night and 1,200 ft AGL subdivisions exist only in Class G. In Class E the same minima apply day and night.
- §91.155(e): an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E airspace area is considered to be within the airspace directly below that area — i.e., at the floor of a Class E shelf you are governed by the Class E (or Class G) rules below, not by the overlying Class E.

ADDITIONAL CLASS E CONSTRAINTS THAT RIDE ALONGSIDE THE TABLE (not substitutes for it)
- §91.155(c): except under Special VFR (§91.157), no VFR flight beneath the ceiling within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport when the ceiling is less than 1,000 ft.
- §91.155(d): except under §91.157, no takeoff, landing, or entry into the traffic pattern under VFR within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area designated for an airport unless ground visibility is at least 3 statute miles, or — if ground visibility is not reported — flight visibility during landing/takeoff/traffic-pattern operation is at least 3 statute miles.
- AIM 3-1-3: where airspace designations overlap, the more restrictive rule governs; Class E is more restrictive than Class G.
- AIM 3-1-4 note: student pilots must also comply with 14 CFR 61.89(a)(6) and (7).
- Special VFR (§91.157) can lower these minima inside the surface area of controlled airspace designated for an airport, with an ATC clearance, clear of clouds, and (for other than helicopters) at least 1 statute mile flight visibility — that is an exception to, not part of, the basic VFR minimums above.

UNIT CONVENTIONS
Visibility in statute miles (U.S. practice); cloud distances in feet.

ONE-LINE ANSWER
In Class E airspace below 10,000 ft MSL, basic VFR requires 3 statute miles flight visibility and cloud clearance of 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, and 2,000 ft horizontally.

# OSHA PEL and Action Level for Respirable Crystalline Silica — General Industry

## Direct answers

| Parameter | Value (8-hour TWA) | Equivalent | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permissible exposure limit (PEL)** | **50 µg/m³** | 0.050 mg/m³ | 29 CFR 1910.1053(c) |
| **Action level (AL)** | **25 µg/m³** | 0.025 mg/m³ | 29 CFR 1910.1053(b), definition of "Action level" |

Both are **8-hour time-weighted averages (TWA)** of airborne respirable crystalline silica, measured in the respirable particle-size fraction. There is **no separate short-term exposure limit (STEL)** and no ceiling value in 1910.1053 — the standard regulates only via the 8-hour TWA PEL and the action level.

Verbatim regulatory text:

- 1910.1053(c) *Permissible exposure limit (PEL).* "The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."
- 1910.1053(b) *Action level* "means a concentration of airborne respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

## Scope — why 1910.1053 is the right section

1910.1053(a)(1) applies to **all occupational exposures to respirable crystalline silica except**:

1. **Construction work** as defined in 29 CFR 1910.12(b) — covered instead by **29 CFR 1926.1153**;
2. **Agricultural operations** covered under 29 CFR part 1928;
3. Exposures resulting from the **processing of sorptive clays**.

Maritime employment is regulated under 29 CFR 1915.1053 / 1917.1053 / 1918.1053, which incorporate the general-industry standard by reference. So for a general-industry facility (manufacturing, foundry, stone countertop fabrication, concrete products, abrasive blasting, etc.), **1910.1053 is the controlling section**, and the two figures above are the ones that apply. If any of the work is construction work, 1926.1153 governs and Table 1 task-based controls may substitute for exposure monitoring — a different compliance path, but the underlying PEL/AL numbers are the same.

## Definitions that determine what the numbers mean

- **Respirable crystalline silica** (1910.1053(b)) means **quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite** contained in airborne particles determined to be respirable by a sampler meeting **ISO 7708:1995** respirable-particle-size-selective characteristics. The single 50 µg/m³ PEL applies to the combined respirable crystalline silica; there is **no separate per-polymorph limit** and no percent-quartz formula adjustment under this section.
- **8-hour TWA** — the concentration averaged over an 8-hour work shift. Exposures on shifts longer than 8 hours must still be evaluated such that the 8-hour TWA does not exceed the PEL; the standard contains no explicit extended-shift adjustment equation, so the averaging convention (and any cumulative-exposure approach used) must be documented in the exposure assessment.

## Threshold ladder — what each number triggers (all values consistent with the two above)

| Exposure condition | Consequence under 1910.1053 |
|---|---|
| Exposure demonstrated by **objective data** to remain **below 25 µg/m³** 8-hr TWA under any foreseeable condition | Standard does not apply — 1910.1053(a)(2). Note this is the same numeric threshold as the AL. |
| Employee is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed **at or above the AL (25 µg/m³)** | Exposure assessment required (1910.1053(d)(1)); **periodic monitoring every 6 months** (d)(3); **medical surveillance offered** if at or above the AL for **30 or more days per year** (i)(1); written exposure control plan required (f)(2). |
| Exposure **above the PEL (50 µg/m³)** | **Periodic monitoring every 3 months** (d)(3); engineering and work-practice controls required to reduce exposures to at or below the PEL (f)(1); **respiratory protection required** where exposures exceed the PEL (g); medical surveillance obligations continue. |
| Any exposure to respirable crystalline silica | Written exposure control plan describing tasks, controls, and housekeeping (f)(2), reviewed at least annually. |

Because the AL (25) is exactly one-half the PEL (50), a monitoring result that lands between them (25 < x ≤ 50) is compliant with the PEL but is **not** a "no action" result: it drives 6-month monitoring, the exposure control plan, and — if sustained 30+ days/year — medical surveillance eligibility.

## Analytical and sampling context (needed to interpret the numbers)

- Air samples must be collected with a respirable-particle-size-selective sampler meeting ISO 7708:1995 (e.g., a cyclone or the GK2.69-type sampler) at the flow rate it was calibrated for, in the employee's breathing zone.
- Analysis is by **X-ray diffraction** per **Appendix A to 1910.1053** (OSHA method ID-142 family), which speciates quartz, cristobalite, and tridymite. Results are reported in µg/m³ of respirable crystalline silica for the sampled period and time-weighted to the 8-hour shift.
- Report results against the 25 and 50 µg/m³ benchmarks, not against the old mppcf convention.

## Historical note (context only — not the answer)

Before the 2016 silica rulemaking, general industry had no substance-specific silica standard; the only limit was the formula in **29 CFR 1910.1000 Table Z-3**, 250 mppcf ÷ (%SiO₂ + 5) for respirable quartz, which for a dust that was nearly pure quartz worked out to roughly 2.4 mppcf — commonly quoted as **approximately** 100 µg/m³. That was a formula, not a fixed PEL, and it is superseded for respirable crystalline silica by the fixed 50 µg/m³ PEL in 1910.1053. The approximate modern equivalent above is offered only to explain why older documents cite a different-looking number; it is not a current compliance limit.

## Jurisdiction caveat

These are the **federal OSHA** values. OSHA-approved **State Plans** must be at least as effective as the federal standard and were required to adopt a silica standard, but the State Plan is the enforceable authority within its jurisdiction and a State Plan may be stricter. Before relying on 50/25 µg/m³ for a specific site, confirm which OSHA jurisdiction covers it (federal OSHA, or a State Plan such as California, Washington, Oregon, Michigan, etc.) and check that plan's adopted text. No State Plan value is asserted here because none was verified.

## One-line answer

For general industry under federal OSHA, 29 CFR 1910.1053: **PEL = 50 µg/m³ (0.050 mg/m³) as an 8-hour TWA; action level = 25 µg/m³ (0.025 mg/m³) as an 8-hour TWA.**

The 1876 first edition of Robert's Rules of Order (the Pocket Manual, transcribed as Project Gutenberg ebook #9097) requires a TWO-THIRDS VOTE to adopt (order) a motion for the Previous Question. It is not a majority vote.

1. WHAT THE 1876 RULE SAYS (paraphrase, not a quotation)

In the 1876 manual the Previous Question is one of the subsidiary motions listed in order of precedence in Part I (Rules of Order), and the manual's article on the Previous Question states the vote required to adopt it: the motion is adopted only on a two-thirds vote. The manual also treats the motion as undebatable and not open to amendment, and it is put in the form 'Shall the main question be now put?' If the two-thirds vote is not obtained, the motion fails and debate on the pending question continues.

I am deliberately giving this as a close paraphrase rather than a verbatim quotation. The passages returned to me by the retrieval step did not include the operative sentence of the 1876 text (see 'Evidence status' below), and inventing quotation marks around a reconstructed sentence would misrepresent the source. The substantive point — two-thirds — is not in doubt.

2. EVIDENCE STATUS AND CONFIDENCE

- Direct grounding obtained: none on the operative sentence. The retrieved pages were (a) the Wikisource table of contents for the 1915 revised edition, which lists '29. The Previous Question ... 104' but does not state the vote requirement in the excerpt captured, and (b) an unrelated Hawaii County record page. Neither contradicts the answer; neither proves it.
- Basis for the answer: the standard text of the 1876 Pocket Manual, plus cross-edition continuity. The two-thirds requirement for the Previous Question appears in the 1876 first edition and is carried forward unchanged through the revised editions (1893, 1904, 1915), where the corresponding section on the Previous Question likewise requires a two-thirds vote. A rule that is stable across five editions is a low-risk answer for the first edition specifically.
- Confidence: high on the value (two-thirds); moderate on the exact sentence wording and on the 1876 article numbering (the 1876 manual's numbering is not the 1915 '§29' numbering, so a citation to '§29' would be an anachronism if applied to 1876).

3. HOW TO VERIFY IN THE GUTENBERG TEXT (procedure for whoever holds the file)

Step 1. Open the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1876 edition (ebook #9097; the HTML file 9097-h.htm is the readable one). Confirm the front matter identifies the 1876 first edition / Pocket Manual rather than a revised edition — check the title page and copyright line, which in the revised editions carry later copyright dates.
Step 2. Search the text for the string 'Previous Question'. Expect several hits: the article devoted to the motion, plus the table of the order of precedence of motions.
Step 3. Read the article on the Previous Question. The sentence to locate is the one stating the vote required for adoption; it states two-thirds. Confirm you are reading the vote to ADOPT the motion, not the vote on the main question.
Step 4. If the transcription is a revised edition (1893 or later), the answer is still two-thirds — the requirement did not change — but the section number will be different and the surrounding procedural details will differ (see caveat below).
Step 5. Record the exact sentence verbatim from that page if a quotation is needed for the deliverable; do not reuse the paraphrase above as a quotation.

4. WHAT THE ANSWER DOES NOT COVER (scope discipline)

- The two-thirds applies to adopting/ordering the Previous Question. It does not change the vote required on the main question itself, which remains whatever that question otherwise requires (ordinarily a majority).
- The two-thirds is a fraction of the votes cast by members voting, which is how the manual's general rule treats a two-thirds vote — flagged as a general-rule point rather than a verified 1876 quotation.
- One genuine first-edition/modern difference, offered as context and not as part of the answer: in the 1876 edition, ordering the Previous Question closed debate on the main question together with the amendments pending to it, whereas later revisions narrowed the motion so that it applies only to the immediately pending question unless the mover specifies otherwise. This affects the EFFECT of the motion, not the two-thirds requirement, and is reported with moderate rather than high confidence.

5. BOTTOM LINE

Vote required to adopt a motion for the Previous Question under the 1876 first edition: two-thirds (2/3) of the votes cast — not a majority, and not unanimous consent.

# Luminous efficacy K_cd in the SI Brochure, 9th edition

## Direct answers

| Ask | Quantity | Fixed value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation, *K*_cd | **683** (exact, by definition) | lm W⁻¹ (= cd sr W⁻¹ = cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³) |
| 2 | Frequency of that monochromatic radiation, ν | **540 × 10¹²** (= 540 THz = 5.4 × 10¹⁴ Hz) | Hz |

Both figures are fixed numerical values in the post-2019 SI: they are exact by definition and carry **no** experimental uncertainty.

## Normative wording (SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2019)

### 1. In the list of the seven defining constants (Chapter 2, section 2.3.1)

> "The International System of Units, the SI, is the system of units in which
> • the unperturbed ground state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium 133 atom ∆ν_Cs is 9 192 631 770 Hz,
> • the speed of light in vacuum c is 299 792 458 m/s,
> • the Planck constant h is 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J s,
> • the elementary charge e is 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C,
> • the Boltzmann constant k is 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J/K,
> • the Avogadro constant N_A is 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ mol⁻¹,
> • **the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² hertz K_cd is 683 lm/W.**"

### 2. In Table 1, "The seven base units of the SI" (candela row)

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, K_cd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹, which is equal to cd sr W⁻¹, or cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ∆ν_Cs."

### 3. The exact relation the definition implies

> "This definition implies the exact relation K_cd = 683 cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 × 10¹² Hz."

### 4. The stated effect of the definition (the candela restated in words)

> "The effect of this definition is that one candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W/sr."

### 5. Inverted relation, for completeness (candela expressed through defining constants)

> 1 cd = (1/683) K_cd (∆ν_Cs)² h · 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ × (9 192 631 770)² ≈ 2.614 830 × 10¹⁰ (∆ν_Cs)² h K_cd

This inversion is the Brochure's own algebra; it is reproduced here only as context and does not alter either fixed value above.

## Points that must not be misread

1. **The defining quantity is a frequency, not a wavelength.** 540 × 10¹² Hz is the fixed specification. Any wavelength is a *derived* value obtained from λ = c/ν = 299 792 458 / (540 × 10¹²) m = 5.551 712 185… × 10⁻⁷ m ≈ 555 nm in vacuum (≈ 555.0 nm in standard air). The familiar "555 nm" figure is a convenience label for the green region near the maximum of the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ); it is **not** part of the definition and must never be substituted for 540 THz when quoting the definition.
2. **No uncertainty is attached.** 683 lm/W is a *fixed numerical value*; the Brochure explicitly states that the definitions specify the exact numerical value of each constant. Do not write "683 ± …".
3. **Unit identity.** 683 lm/W = 683 cd sr W⁻¹ = 683 cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³. These are the same value expressed in three equivalent unit forms used in the Brochure; the numerical value 683 is unchanged.
4. **Provenance and version.** The values derive from the 26th CGPM (2018), which revised the SI to be based on fixed numerical values of seven defining constants; the 9th edition of the *SI Brochure* (BIPM, 2019) is the text that carries the revised definitions. The same 683 / 540 × 10¹² Hz pairing appears already in the draft of the ninth Brochure dated 5 February 2018, in the published 9th edition Table 1, and in the BIPM concise summary of the 9th edition — three mutually consistent BIPM sources, so no revision-dependent discrepancy exists for these two values. (Later corrigenda to the 9th edition correct typographical and cross-reference errors; they do not change defining constants, which are fixed by CGPM resolution and are not editable by the Brochure.)
5. **Prior SI status (for contrast only).** Before the 2019 revision the candela was defined via a 540 × 10¹² Hz monochromatic source of radiant intensity 1/683 W/sr; the 2019 wording converts this to a fixed value of *K*_cd. The number and the frequency are unchanged by that rewording — which is why both the pre- and post-2019 formulations yield the same two answers requested here.

## Verification checklist

- [x] Value of *K*_cd stated as 683 — matches all three fetched BIPM passages.
- [x] Unit stated as lm W⁻¹ — matches the defining-constants list; equivalent forms cd sr W⁻¹ and cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ match Table 1 and section 2.3.1.
- [x] Frequency stated as 540 × 10¹² Hz — matches all three fetched BIPM passages, and is stated as a frequency in every one of them.
- [x] No uncertainty attached to either number (both exact by definition).
- [x] No wavelength presented as the defining quantity; the ≈555 nm figure is explicitly flagged as derived and non-normative.
- [x] The two reported values appear together in a single quoted sentence, so they cannot have been drawn from different, mismatched contexts.

# Compliance Determination — Transport Classification of a Liquid with Flash Point 65 °C (149 °F)

**Scope:** U.S. DOT / PHMSA hazardous materials regulations, 49 CFR Parts 171–180, domestic transport, material offered at ambient temperature in the condition described. Prepared by the Compliance Engineer.

---

## 1. Answer (verdict)

**No. The liquid is not a Class 3 flammable liquid.**

Under 49 CFR 173.120(a) a Class 3 flammable liquid is a liquid with a flash point of **not more than 60 °C (140 °F)**. This material's flash point is **65 °C (149 °F)**, which is 5 °C above the Class 3 ceiling, so it fails the defining test.

**What it is:** a **combustible liquid** under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1) — "any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F)." The stated flash point (65 °C) lies strictly between 60 °C and 93 °C, and the request stipulates that the material meets no other hazard class.

**Regulatory consequence:** "combustible liquid" is a defined term, not a hazard class. Class 3 is the hazard class (49 CFR 171.8: "Class 3. See § 173.120"). A material that is only a combustible liquid does not meet the defining criteria of any hazard class in Part 173 and is therefore **not a hazardous material for transport** — provided the independent checks in §5 below all come back negative. No shipping paper, Class 3 label, placard, emergency response information, or Part 172/173 packaging authorization is required for it as such.

Two conditions must be confirmed before that conclusion is relied on: (a) the 65 °C figure is a valid **closed-cup** result from a method listed in 173.120(c)(1); and (b) the material is **not** intentionally heated and offered/transported at or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging (see §4.1).

---

## 2. Governing regulatory text (verbatim, as retrieved)

**49 CFR 173.120(a) — Flammable liquid:**
> "a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions: (1) Any liquid meeting one of the definitions specified in § 173.115. (2) Any mixture having one or more components with a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher, that make up at least 99 percent of the total volume of the mixture, if the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point. (3) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) that does not sustain combustion according to ASTM D 4206 … (4) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) and with a fire point greater than 100 °C (212 °F) according to ISO 2592 … (5) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) which is in a water-miscible solution with a water content of more than 90 percent by mass."

**49 CFR 173.120(b) — Combustible liquid:**
> "(1) … a combustible liquid means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F). (2) A flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class may be reclassed as a combustible liquid. This provision does not apply to transportation by vessel or aircraft, except where other means of transportation is impracticable. An elevated temperature material that meets the definition of a Class 3 material because it is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point may not be reclassed as a combustible liquid."

**49 CFR 173.120(c)(1) — Flash point determination:** closed-cup methods only — ASTM D 56 (Tag CC), ASTM D 3278 (small-scale CC), ASTM D 93 (Pensky-Martens CC), ISO 1516, ISO 1523, ISO 2719, ISO 3679, ISO 3680, ISO 13736 (Abel CC), selected by viscosity/surface-film characteristics.

**49 CFR 171.8 — Elevated temperature material:** bulk packaging and (1) liquid phase at ≥ 100 °C; or (2) liquid phase with flash point ≥ 38 °C intentionally heated and offered/transported at or above its flash point; or (3) solid phase at ≥ 240 °C.

---

## 3. Classification walk-through (decision record)

| Step | Question | Basis | Result for this material |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is it a liquid? Melting/initial melting point ≤ 20 °C at 101.3 kPa (or fluidity per ASTM D 4359 / ADR 2.3.4 for viscous materials) | 171.8 "Liquid" | Assumed yes (a flash point determination presupposes a liquid). **Confirm on the test report.** |
| 2 | Is the 65 °C figure from an acceptable method? | 173.120(c)(1) | Must be closed cup: ASTM D 56, D 3278, D 93, or ISO 1516/1523/2719/3679/3680/13736. **Open-cup results (e.g., ASTM D 1310, Cleveland open cup) are not an acceptable basis** and are typically several degrees higher than closed cup. Assumed valid per the project assumptions. |
| 3 | Flash point ≤ 60 °C? | 173.120(a) prong 1 | **No — 65 °C > 60 °C. Fails.** Not Class 3 on this prong. |
| 4 | Elevated-temperature override: liquid phase, flash point ≥ 37.8 °C, intentionally heated, offered/transported at or above flash point, in a bulk packaging? | 173.120(a) prong 2; 171.8 | 65 °C ≥ 37.8 °C, so the flash-point condition is met; the answer turns entirely on bulk packaging + heating. **Assumed not heated, not bulk-heated → override not triggered.** See §4.1. |
| 5 | Do the 173.120(a)(1)–(5) exceptions apply? | 173.120(a)(1)–(5) | Moot. Exceptions (2)–(5) exist only to remove a material that would otherwise be Class 3; a 65 °C material never enters Class 3. (a)(1) (a Class 2 gas definition) is not implicated. Record them anyway in the file, since they show the material would remain outside Class 3 even if the flash point were lower. |
| 6 | Is it a combustible liquid? Flash point > 60 °C and < 93 °C, and no other hazard class | 173.120(b)(1) | **Yes.** 60 °C < 65 °C < 93 °C, and no other hazard class per the request. |
| 7 | Does "combustible liquid" make it a hazardous material? | 171.8 "Hazardous material"; Part 173 class definitions | **No, not by itself.** Combustible liquid is not a hazard class. Regulated only if an independent trigger in §5 applies. |
| 8 | Packing group | 173.121 | **None / not applicable** — packing groups are assigned only to Class 3 material. |

**Note on a common error:** 173.120(b)(2) (reclassing a flammable liquid with flash point ≥ 38 °C as a combustible liquid) is **not** the provision that classifies this material. (b)(2) only converts a material that is *already* Class 3. A 65 °C material is a combustible liquid under (b)(1) directly, without any reclassing election.

---

## 4. Facts that would change the answer

### 4.1 Elevated-temperature transport (the only realistic path back into Class 3)
If the material is (i) in a **bulk packaging**, (ii) **intentionally heated**, and (iii) offered for transportation or transported **at or above 65 °C**, it **is Class 3** under the second prong of 173.120(a), and is also an **elevated temperature material** under 171.8. It then may **not** be reclassed as a combustible liquid (173.120(b)(2), last sentence), and requires the Class 3 (or elevated-temperature, as applicable) shipping description, packaging, marking, and placarding. Packing group is assigned under 173.121; for a material that is Class 3 solely because it is an elevated temperature material, the practical assignment is PG III — **confirm the current 173.121 text before using it on a shipping paper.** Non-bulk packages heated above flash point do not trigger the Class 3 prong, because both 173.120(a) and the 171.8 definition require a bulk packaging.

### 4.2 Flash-point data risk
65 °C is only 5 °C above the 60 °C ceiling. Apply the repeatability/reproducibility of the method used (per the ASTM/ISO standard's precision section) to the reported result. If the lower precision bound of the result falls at or below 60 °C, the defensible call is to **classify as Class 3 (PG III) or retest**, not to rely on the single number. Record the method, apparatus, laboratory, sample identification, date, and precision statement in the classification file.

### 4.3 Sensitivity table

| If, in fact… | Then… | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Closed-cup flash point is ≤ 60 °C | Class 3; PG III for flash point 23–60 °C with initial boiling point > 35 °C; may be reclassed as combustible under (b)(2) if flash point ≥ 38 °C and not vessel/air | 173.120(a), 173.121, 173.120(b)(2) |
| Bulk + intentionally heated to ≥ 65 °C | Class 3 (elevated temperature); no combustible reclass | 173.120(a), 171.8, 173.120(b)(2) |
| Flash point ≥ 93 °C (200 °F) | Neither Class 3 nor a combustible liquid; still screen §5 triggers | 173.120(b)(1) |
| Does not sustain combustion (ASTM D 4206 or Part 173 App. H) and flash point > 35 °C | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(3) — already outside | 173.120(a)(3) |
| Fire point > 100 °C per ISO 2592 and flash point > 35 °C | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(4) — already outside | 173.120(a)(4) |
| Water-miscible solution, > 90 % water by mass, flash point > 35 °C | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(5) — already outside | 173.120(a)(5) |
| Mixture: ≥ 99 vol % of components have flash point ≥ 60 °C, and not transported at/above flash point | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(2) — already outside | 173.120(a)(2) |
| Offered by vessel or aircraft | (b)(2) reclass unavailable; verify modal rules — but 65 °C closed cup exceeds the 60 °C Class 3 cutoff in IMDG/IATA/UN Model Regulations as well, so still not Class 3 absent heating | 173.120(b)(2); IMDG 2.3.1; IATA DGR 3.3 |

---

## 5. Independent triggers that would make it a hazardous material anyway

"Meets no other hazard class" does **not** by itself mean "not regulated." Confirm each of the following and document the result:

1. **Listed by name in the §172.101 Hazardous Materials Table.** If the material is a named substance, the HMT entry governs regardless of flash point. (The Table also contains domestic combustible-liquid entries such as "Combustible liquid, n.o.s."; verify the current entry and its conditions if a description is ever needed.)
2. **CERCLA hazardous substance** (40 CFR 302; 49 CFR 172.101 Appendix A) — regulated as a hazardous material when shipped in one package at or above its reportable quantity.
3. **Marine pollutant** (49 CFR 172.101 Appendix B; 171.8) — triggers marking and shipping-paper requirements under the HMR independent of mode.
4. **Hazardous waste** (40 CFR 261; 171.8) — a hazardous waste is a hazardous material regardless of its physical/flammability characteristics.
5. **Elevated temperature material** (171.8) — bulk + ≥ 100 °C liquid, or bulk + flash point ≥ 38 °C heated to/above flash point, or bulk + solid ≥ 240 °C.
6. **Any other hazard class** — verify the "no other class" assertion against Classes 1–9, not just flammability: pH/corrosivity (Class 8), acute toxicity (Class 6.1), oxidizing/combustion-supporting behavior (Class 5.1), self-heating (Class 4.2), etc.

If all six are negative, the material is not subject to the HMR.

---

## 6. Documentation package for the classification file

1. Flash point test report — method from 173.120(c)(1), closed cup, apparatus, lab, sample ID, date, result 65 °C, and the method's precision statement.
2. Melting point / fluidity determination supporting the "liquid" definition (171.8).
3. Composition and hazard-class screening memo covering Classes 1–9.
4. Statement of the offering condition: ambient temperature, packaging type (non-bulk vs bulk), and confirmation that the material is not intentionally heated to or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging.
5. Appendix A (CERCLA) and Appendix B (marine pollutant) screens; hazardous-waste determination if applicable.
6. Written classification determination signed and dated, stating: "Flash point 65 °C closed cup (method ___). Not a Class 3 flammable liquid per 49 CFR 173.120(a); combustible liquid per 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1); not subject to the HMR as a hazardous material."
7. Re-evaluation trigger: any change in formulation, supplier, test method, or offering temperature requires re-determination.

---

## 7. What goes on the documents

- **Shipping paper:** none required; no proper shipping name, hazard class, UN number, or emergency response telephone number is mandated. A carrier-required notation is acceptable and common, e.g. "Not regulated — combustible liquid, flash point 65 °C (149 °F) closed cup." Do **not** apply a Class 3 label, a Class 3 hazard class designation, or placards.
- **SDS Section 14:** "US DOT: Not regulated as a hazardous material (combustible liquid, flash point 65 °C / 149 °F closed cup; above the 60 °C Class 3 threshold)." This is *not* inconsistent with Section 2 — the two regimes use different cutoffs; say so explicitly in the SDS to preempt auditor questions.

---

## 8. Adjacent regimes (the SDS will classify it differently — this is expected)

| Regime | Classification at flash point 65 °C (149 °F) | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| US DOT transport (49 CFR) | Combustible liquid; not a Class 3 flammable liquid; not regulated as a hazardous material absent §5 triggers | 173.120(a), (b)(1) |
| OSHA HazCom / GHS | **Flammable liquid, Category 4** (flash point > 60 °C and ≤ 93 °C); H227 "Combustible liquid"; no pictogram, no signal word | 29 CFR 1910.1200 App. B / GHS criteria |
| NFPA 30 / 29 CFR 1910.106 | **Class IIIA combustible liquid** (≥ 140 °F and < 200 °F) | 1910.106(a)(18) |
| IMDG / IATA / UN Model Regs | Not Class 3 (above 60 °C closed cup) unless transported at or above its flash point | IMDG 2.3.1; IATA DGR 3.3 |
