# NRC public dose limits — annual and any-one-hour, unrestricted area

## 1. Answer at a glance

| # | Limit | Citation | Quantity | Value (US) | Value (SI) |
|---|-------|----------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| **A** | **Annual public dose limit** | **10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1)** | Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE), all pathways, from the licensed operation | **0.1 rem in a year** (100 mrem/yr) | **1 mSv/yr** |
| **B** | **Any-one-hour limit in an unrestricted area** | **10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2)** | Dose **from external sources** in any unrestricted area | **0.002 rem in any one hour** (2 mrem/h) | **0.02 mSv (20 µSv) in any one hour** |

The directly asked figure — *any one hour in an unrestricted area* — is **0.002 rem per hour (0.02 mSv/h; 2 mrem/h; 20 µSv/h)**. The companion annual figure is **0.1 rem (1 mSv) per year** TEDE.

These are two independent limits. Both must be satisfied simultaneously; neither is a proration of the other.

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text

10 CFR 20.1301 (Subpart D — Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public), paragraphs (a) and (b):

> **§ 20.1301 Dose limits for individual members of the public.**
>
> (a) Each licensee shall conduct operations so that—
>
> (1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and
>
> (2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.
>
> (b) If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those individuals.

Source history: 56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991; amended at 60 FR 48625 (Sept. 20, 1995); 62 FR 4133 (Jan. 29, 1997); 67 FR 20370 (Apr. 24, 2002); 67 FR 62872 (Oct. 9, 2002). Text above is the current eCFR text and matches the 2025 printed CFR (10 CFR Ch. I, 1–1–25 Edition, p. 358).

## 3. Scope difference between the two limits — the point most often gotten wrong

| | Annual limit, (a)(1) | Hourly limit, (a)(2) |
|---|---|---|
| Dose quantity | TEDE (external + committed effective dose equivalent from inhalation/ingestion) | Dose from **external sources only** |
| Pathway coverage | All pathways from the licensed operation, including effluent releases | Direct external exposure (gamma, x-ray, beta, neutron) only |
| Where it applies | To the **individual** member of the public (the maximally exposed individual) | To the **area** — any unrestricted area, whether or not anyone is present |
| Time basis | Calendar year | Any single clock hour; **no averaging over a year is permitted** |
| Occupancy assumption | Actual/assumed occupancy of the maximally exposed individual | Evaluated as if an individual were present for that hour |

Consequences to state plainly to a licensee:

- There is **no one-hour limit for internal dose**. Short-term control of internal dose is achieved indirectly, through the annual-average effluent concentration limits of appendix B, table 2 (see §20.1302(b)(2)(i)) and through ALARA.
- The hourly limit is an **area** limit and is not satisfied by controlling access. If the dose rate anywhere in an unrestricted area exceeds 2 mrem/h (20 µSv/h), the licensee is out of compliance even if no one is there. The remedy is shielding, distance, source relocation, or reclassifying the area as controlled (with the access controls that implies) — not a sign or an administrative control alone.
- Conversely, meeting 2 mrem/h everywhere does **not** demonstrate compliance with the annual limit; a location at exactly 2 mrem/h occupied continuously would yield ~17.5 rem/yr (0.002 rem/h × 8,766 h = 17.53 rem = 175 mSv), seventeen times the annual limit. This is precisely why the two limits coexist: the annual limit governs chronic low-level exposure, the hourly limit catches localized high dose rates (shielded-source failures, hot spots, mispositioned sources, collimator or cask leakage).

## 4. Exclusions and inclusions

**Excluded from the annual 0.1 rem (1 mSv) limit** — these dose contributions are not counted against the licensee:

1. Background radiation.
2. Any medical administration the individual has received (diagnostic or therapeutic).
3. Exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under §35.75 (i.e., released patients are not the licensee's dose burden).
4. Voluntary participation in medical research programs.
5. The licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with §20.2003.

**Excluded from the hourly 0.002 rem limit**: dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with §35.75. (Note the asymmetry — the hourly exclusion list is narrower; background is not expressly listed in (a)(2), but the limit is on dose *from the licensed operation* and natural background is not a licensee contribution.)

**Included**: dose to members of the public who are permitted access to controlled areas — §20.1301(b) keeps the public limits applicable to those individuals.

## 5. Exceptions and alternate limits (do not confuse these with the default)

| Provision | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| §20.1301(c) — visitors to a patient who cannot be released under §35.75 | Up to **0.5 rem (5 mSv)** | Only for visitors of such a patient; the authorized user (10 CFR Part 35) must determine **before the visit** that it is appropriate. This is a per-visit authorization, not a standing annual allowance. |
| §20.1301(d) — alternate annual limit | Up to **0.5 rem (5 mSv) per year** | Requires **prior NRC authorization**; application must contain (1) demonstration of need and expected duration of operations above the 0.1 rem limit, (2) the program to assess and control dose within the 0.5 rem limit, and (3) procedures to maintain dose ALARA. This is the only route by which the annual public limit may lawfully be exceeded; it does not exist as an as-of-right option. |
| §20.1301(e) | — | A licensee also subject to EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in 40 CFR part 190 must comply with those as well. |
| §20.1301(f) | — | The Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on total radionuclide quantities released, to restrict collective dose. |

**Important:** there is no provision anywhere in Part 20 that permits averaging the 0.002 rem/h limit over a year, over a day, or over a shift. The 0.5 rem/yr figure in (d) is an *annual* alternative and does not relax (a)(2); a licensee operating under (d) is still bound by 0.002 rem in any one hour.

## 6. How compliance is demonstrated — §20.1302

§20.1302(a): the licensee must make surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and of radioactive materials in effluents released to those areas, to demonstrate compliance with §20.1301.

§20.1302(b) offers two compliance routes for the annual limit:

- **(b)(1)** Demonstrate by measurement or calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation does not exceed the annual limit (the maximally exposed individual / MEI approach); **or**
- **(b)(2)** Demonstrate both of the following:
  - (i) annual average concentrations of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed appendix B, table 2 values; **and**
  - (ii) **if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area**, the dose from external sources would not exceed **0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour and 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year**.

Two practical notes for the one-hour figure:

- A calibrated survey instrument reading of **2 mrem/h (20 µSv/h)** at the unrestricted-area boundary is the compliance boundary. A reading at or below 2 mrem/h, sustained for the full hour, meets (a)(2); anything above it is a violation in that hour regardless of duration.
- The (b)(2)(ii) external-only annual figure of **0.05 rem (0.5 mSv)** is exactly half the 0.1 rem TEDE limit — the other half is implicitly reserved for the internal (inhalation/ingestion) pathway. 0.05 rem/yr ÷ 8,766 h = **5.7 µrem/h (0.057 µSv/h)**, which is far below 2 mrem/h, so for continuous occupancy the annual external criterion governs and the hourly limit is not the binding constraint.

## 7. Definitions that fix the scope (10 CFR 20.1003)

- **Unrestricted area** — an area to which access is neither limited by the licensee for purposes of protecting individuals from exposure to radiation and radioactive materials, nor any area used for residential quarters. (Paraphrase of §20.1003; consult the current definitional text for exact wording when drafting.)
- **Member of the public** — any individual, except when that individual is receiving an occupational dose. Occupational dose is governed by Subpart C (§§20.1201–20.1208: 5 rem/yr TEDE, etc.), not by §20.1301. This is the dividing line: the same person can be an occupationally exposed worker on site and a member of the public off site, but not both for the same exposure.
- **Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE)** — the sum of the deep-dose equivalent (external) and the committed effective dose equivalent (internal), as defined in §20.1003.

## 8. Related but distinct limits (context, not answers to the question)

These are frequently conflated with §20.1301 in licensee discussions. They are separate requirements:

- **ALARA, §20.1101(b)** — the licensee must make every reasonable effort to maintain public and occupational doses ALARA, i.e., well below the §20.1301 limits. ALARA is an obligation on the licensee, not a numerical public limit.
- **Air-emission constraint, §20.1101(d)** — a 10 mrem/yr (0.1 mSv/yr) constraint on radionuclide emissions to ambient air for the licensees to which that paragraph applies (the 40 CFR part 61, subpart I interface). Confirm the current applicability conditions before citing it in a licensing document.
- **Effluent concentration limits, appendix B, table 2 to Part 20** — annual-average concentration limits at the unrestricted-area boundary; used as a compliance route under §20.1302(b)(2)(i).
- **EPA fuel-cycle standards, 40 CFR part 190** — 25 mrem/yr whole-body TEDE, 75 mrem/yr thyroid, 25 mrem/yr any other organ, for the uranium fuel cycle; incorporated by §20.1301(e).
- **EPA NESHAP, 40 CFR part 61, subpart I** — 10 mrem/yr effective dose and 3 mrem/yr iodine-131, for designated facilities.

## 9. Jurisdiction and applicability

- The limits above are those of the **U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission** under **10 CFR Part 20**, the NRC's primary radiation-protection rule.
- **Agreement States** adopt compatible regulations under their own citations; the numerical limits are, in practice, the same (typically 0.1 rem/yr and 0.002 rem/h), but the citable authority in an Agreement State is the State regulation, not 10 CFR 20.1301.
- §20.1301 applies to **NRC licensees** (and to persons holding a license or applying for one, per (d)). It does not set limits for background, for medical exposure of patients (that is a Part 35 / FDA matter), or for non-licensed sources.

## 10. Assumptions made in answering (correct these if they are wrong for your use)

1. The requester wants the limits as stated in **10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D**, current as of the eCFR text retrieved 2026-11-17 — not another framework (e.g., DOE Order 458.1, which sets 100 mrem/yr for DOE operations, or ICRP recommendations).
2. "Dose" for the annual limit means **TEDE**; "dose" for the hourly limit means **dose from external sources**.
3. "Unrestricted area" is used in the §20.1003 sense, and the question is the general regulatory-knowledge question, not a specific licensee's licensing basis.
4. NRC jurisdiction (not Agreement State, not another federal agency).
5. The requester wants the **regulatory limits themselves**, not licensee-set dose constraints or NRC guidance values (e.g., the lower administrative constraint values found in some license conditions).

## 11. Bottom line for a one-line citation

> Under 10 CFR 20.1301(a), an NRC licensee must conduct operations so that (1) the total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public does not exceed **0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year**, and (2) the dose in any unrestricted area from external sources does not exceed **0.002 rem (0.02 mSv; 2 mrem; 20 µSv) in any one hour**.

# Compliance Determination — Alcohol Concentration Bar for US CMV Drivers

## 1. Determination (the answer)

A driver of a commercial motor vehicle is barred from reporting for duty or remaining on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions at an **alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater**.

The threshold is **inclusive**: 0.04 itself bars duty. The unit of measure under the federal program is **grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (g/210 L BrAC)**, as indicated by an evidential breath test conducted under 49 CFR Part 40.

- Controlling authority: **49 CFR § 382.201 (Alcohol concentration)**, Part 382, Subpart B (Prohibitions), FMCSA.
- Current text (eCFR, verified):

> § 382.201 Alcohol concentration.
> No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions.
> [66 FR 43103, Aug. 17, 2001, as amended at 77 FR 4483, Jan. 30, 2012]

The rule is bilateral: it prohibits the **driver** from reporting/remaining on duty, and separately prohibits the **employer** from permitting the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions once the employer has knowledge of a 0.04-or-greater result. (The 2012 amendment at 77 FR 4483 changed the employer standard in § 382.201 from "actual knowledge" to "knowledge"; § 382.205 and § 382.207 retain "actual knowledge" language.)

## 2. Measurement basis and definition

"Alcohol concentration" (or "alcohol content") is defined in **49 CFR § 382.107** and **49 CFR § 40.3** as the alcohol in a volume of breath expressed in terms of grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath as indicated by an evidential breath test under the rule. Practical consequences of that definition:

1. The federal program's operative measurement is **breath**, taken on an evidential breath testing device (EBT) that appears on the ODAPC conforming-products list and meets Part 40 calibration/maintenance requirements.
2. **Blood test results are not DOT test results.** A hospital or law-enforcement blood draw may support a state criminal case or an employer's independent action, but it does not establish a § 382.201 violation for purposes of the DOT program. Do not convert a blood result into a breath figure and treat it as a DOT test result.
3. A 0.04 BrAC corresponds to a whole-blood alcohol concentration of roughly 0.04 g/dL under the standard 2100:1 breath-to-blood partition ratio, but the federal bar is expressed and enforced in breath units.

## 3. Threshold table — do not conflate these

| Result (BrAC) | Regulatory characterization | Required action |
|---|---|---|
| 0.00 – 0.019 | Negative / below all thresholds | No action; driver may perform safety-sensitive functions (subject to §§ 382.205, 382.207, 382.209 below). |
| 0.02 – 0.039 | **Not** a § 382.201 violation, but a removal trigger under § 382.505 (Subpart E) | Driver may not perform or continue safety-sensitive functions until the return-to-duty process in § 382.503 is completed (SAP evaluation, return-to-duty test < 0.02, follow-up testing). |
| **0.04 or greater** | **Violation of § 382.201** — the bar asked about | Immediate removal from safety-sensitive functions; SAP referral under § 382.501(c); no return until § 382.503 process complete. |

Note on the 0.02 line: 0.02 is a **testing/removal** threshold, not the answer to the question posed. It is lower than 0.04 and does not modify it. The 0.04 figure is the concentration at which the driver is barred by the prohibition itself.

## 4. How a result is established (Part 40 procedure)

1. **Screening test** on an approved alcohol screening device or EBT. A screening result of **0.02 or greater** requires a **confirmation test**; a screening result below 0.02 is treated as negative.
2. **Confirmation test** on an EBT, administered after the required waiting period (at least 15 minutes, and no more than 30 minutes, after the screening test) and without any substance ingested in the interim.
3. **The confirmation test result is the result of record.** A screening result alone never supports a § 382.201 violation.
4. Tests must be conducted by a trained BAT/STT under 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart J (alcohol testing), with the alcohol testing form (ATF) completed; the driver's CDL number and State of issuance are recorded per § 382.403(b).
5. **Refusal to test** is treated as a violation equivalent to a 0.04-or-greater result (§ 382.211) and triggers the same removal and SAP process.

## 5. Bars that operate independently of concentration

These prohibit safety-sensitive duty regardless of any measured concentration and should not be read as lowering the numeric threshold:

- **§ 382.205 — On-duty use.** No driver may use alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions.
- **§ 382.207 — Pre-duty use.** No driver may perform safety-sensitive functions **within four hours after using alcohol**.
- **§ 382.209 — Use following an accident.** A driver required to take a post-accident alcohol test may not use alcohol for **eight hours** following the accident, or until an alcohol test is administered, whichever occurs first.
- **§ 382.211 — Refusal to submit** to a required test.
- **§ 382.213 / § 382.215 — Controlled substance use**, including Schedule I drugs and non-Schedule I drugs outside a licensed practitioner's instruction.

A driver who has consumed any alcohol within four hours is barred even at a measured concentration of 0.00. Compliance programs must therefore enforce the timing rules and the 0.04 line as separate controls.

## 6. Employer obligations and consequences of a ≥ 0.04 result

1. **Remove** the driver from safety-sensitive functions immediately — including driving — and do not permit performance or continued performance (§ 382.201, § 382.501).
2. **Refer** the driver to a **Substance Abuse Professional** (§ 382.501(c)); the SAP performs the evaluation and prescribes education/treatment.
3. **Return-to-duty** only after the SAP process is complete and the driver passes a **return-to-duty alcohol test with a result of less than 0.02** (§ 382.309), conducted under direct observation.
4. **Follow-up testing** as prescribed by the SAP: at least **six** tests in the first **twelve** months of return to duty, and continuation for up to **60 months** (§ 382.311), with alcohol follow-up tests under direct observation.
5. **Recordkeeping**: alcohol test records are maintained under § 382.401; violation and return-to-duty information is reported to and queried from the **FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse** (§ 382.601–382.609 series, including the CDL-holder consent and query requirements).
6. **Driver education materials** must be distributed under § 382.601, describing the 0.04 prohibition and the consequences.
7. **Testing program context** (not thresholds): random alcohol testing at a minimum annual rate of **10%** of average driver positions and random controlled-substances testing at **50%** (§ 382.305); post-accident alcohol testing attempted within **8 hours** of the accident, with attempts ceasing and documentation made if not administered within that window (§ 382.303); pre-employment alcohol testing is optional, but if conducted must follow Part 40 (§ 382.301(c)).

## 7. Interaction with state law

Many states impose their own CMV alcohol limits and penalties (some at 0.04, some at 0.02, plus separate "implied consent" and criminal provisions). The **federal** bar under Part 382 is 0.04. Part 382 preempts state or local requirements that are inconsistent with or that impose additional testing requirements on employers covered by Part 382 (§ 382.109), but state criminal law, licensing sanctions, and out-of-service criteria applied by enforcement officers operate independently of the federal testing program. A state limit below 0.04 does not change the answer to this question; it changes the driver's exposure to state penalties.

## 8. Audit / verification checklist

- [ ] Written policy states the **0.04 or greater** prohibition verbatim in substance, and separately states the 0.02 removal rule.
- [ ] Policy states the four-hour pre-duty rule and the eight-hour post-accident rule as independent bars.
- [ ] Supervisors trained on reasonable-suspicion testing (§ 382.307) and on the immediate-removal duty.
- [ ] Only EBTs on the ODAPC conforming-products list are used; calibration and BAT training records current.
- [ ] Confirmation test performed and its result — not the screening result — recorded as the result of record.
- [ ] SAP referral, return-to-duty test result **< 0.02**, and follow-up testing schedule documented in the driver's file.
- [ ] Clearinghouse query/reporting obligations satisfied for any § 382.201 violation.

## 9. Common errors this determination corrects

1. Answering **0.02** — that is the confirmation-testing and removal threshold under § 382.505, not the § 382.201 prohibition.
2. Answering **0.08** — the common state DUI per-se limit; it does not govern CMV drivers under Part 382.
3. Treating 0.04 as exclusive ("more than 0.04") — the regulation says "0.04 **or greater**."
4. Using a blood test result as the DOT result — the federal program is a breath-test program.
5. Believing a driver under 0.04 is always clear to drive — the four-hour pre-duty rule, the on-duty-use rule, and the eight-hour post-accident rule bar duty regardless of concentration.

## 10. Sources

- 49 CFR § 382.201, eCFR (current): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-382/subpart-B/section-382.201
- 49 CFR Part 382, GovInfo CFR 2022 compilations (§§ 382.201, 382.205, 382.207, 382.209): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2022-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2022-title49-vol5-part382.pdf
- 49 CFR Part 382, GovInfo CFR 2023 compilation (§§ 382.201, 382.211, 382.213): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2023-title49-vol5-sec382-207.pdf
- 49 CFR § 382.201, GovInfo CFR 2006 XML (historical continuity of the 0.04 threshold): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2006-title49-vol5/xml/CFR-2006-title49-vol5-sec382-201.xml
- Related provisions cited by section number: 49 CFR §§ 382.107 (definitions), 382.109 (preemption), 382.211, 382.301, 382.303, 382.305, 382.307, 382.309, 382.311, 382.401, 382.403, 382.501, 382.503, 382.505, 382.601; 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart J (alcohol testing procedures) and § 40.3 (definitions).

**Bottom line: 0.04 g/210 L breath, inclusive — a CMV driver may not report for or remain on duty requiring safety-sensitive functions at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater (49 CFR § 382.201).**

# Statutory paid annual leave — Great Britain

## Answer

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Statutory minimum paid annual leave | **5.6 weeks** per leave year |
| Statutory cap on that entitlement | **28 days** |

For the standard five-day week the two figures coincide: 5.6 × 5 = 28 days. The cap is an absolute ceiling on the statutory entitlement, so it only reduces the weeks' worth of leave for someone working more than five days a week (e.g. a six-day week: 5.6 × 6 = 33.6, cut to 28 days, i.e. 4.67 weeks' worth).

## Legal basis

- **Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), reg 13(1):** a worker is entitled to **4 weeks'** annual leave in each leave year (as substituted by SI 2001/3256).
- **Reg 13A(2)(e):** for any leave year beginning on or after 1 April 2009, a worker is entitled to a further **1.6 weeks'** additional annual leave (introduced by SI 2007/2079).
- **Reg 13A(3):** "The aggregate entitlement provided for in paragraph (2) and regulation 13(1) is subject to a maximum of **28 days**."
- **Arithmetic:** 4 weeks + 1.6 weeks = **5.6 weeks**; 5.6 × 5 days = **28 days**.
- **GOV.UK confirms** the same: "Almost all people classed as workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year"; "Most workers who work a 5-day week must receive at least 28 days' paid annual leave a year"; "Statutory paid holiday entitlement is limited to 28 days."

## Scope and interpretation

1. **"Worker".** The WTR definition covers employees and limb (b) workers — agency workers, zero-hours workers, workers with irregular hours, and part-year workers are all within the 5.6 weeks. If the questioner meant only "employee", the answer is unchanged, because every employee is a worker for these purposes.
2. **Great Britain.** England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998; the headline figures are the same but NI is outside the scope of this answer. The agriculture provisions in reg 13(4) and Schedule 2 (Wales/Scotland) and the Agricultural Wages (Scotland) Act 1949 carve-out in reg 13A(8) affect how leave is set for those workers, not the 5.6-week/28-day baseline for workers generally.
3. **Statutory minimum only.** 5.6 weeks is a floor. Contracts commonly give more (e.g. 25 days plus bank holidays); that extra leave is contractual and is not governed by the WTR rules on carry-over, pay and remedy. Check the contract first.
4. **Bank holidays.** There is no statutory right to bank or public holidays off. An employer may count bank holidays towards the 28 days, so a worker given "20 days plus 8 bank holidays" receives exactly the 28-day statutory minimum and nothing more.
5. **Leave year.** Reg 13(3): the leave year begins on the date set by a relevant agreement, or (absent agreement) on the anniversary of the employment start date (1 October 1998 for employment beginning on or before that date). The definition affects accrual and timing, not the 5.6-week/28-day figures.
6. **2024 amendment.** The Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1426) inserted reg 13(A1) and reg 15B. For leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024, irregular-hours and part-year workers accrue leave at 12.07% of hours worked (with rolled-up holiday pay permitted), but the entitlement remains 5.6 weeks subject to the 28-day cap. For other workers, reg 13 and 13A apply as before.

## Calculation rule

For a worker with regular hours and fixed-length days, full leave year:

> **Statutory entitlement (days) = the lower of (a) 28 days, or (b) 5.6 × days worked per week.**

Worked examples:

| Days worked per week | 5.6 × days | Entitlement | Equivalent weeks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 28.0 | 28.0 days | 5.6 weeks |
| 4 | 22.4 | 22.4 days | 5.6 weeks |
| 3 | 16.8 | 16.8 days | 5.6 weeks |
| 6 | 33.6 | **28.0 days** (cap applies) | 4.67 weeks |

- Part-time workers working regular hours all year get 5.6 weeks, which is fewer than 28 days.
- Shift workers: 5.6 weeks of the average working week, capped at 28 days' worth of shifts.
- Irregular-hours and part-year workers: from 1 April 2024, 12.07% of hours worked in the pay period, subject to the same 28-day ceiling.
- Starting or leaving part-way through a leave year: entitlement accrues pro rata (1/12 of the annual entitlement per month, or 12.07% of hours for irregular-hours workers).

## Practical HR notes

- **Holiday pay** (reg 16) must be at the worker's normal remuneration rate — regular overtime, commission and allowances that are normally paid should be reflected; the 5.6 weeks is leave, and it must be paid leave to count.
- **Record-keeping:** employers must keep records sufficient to show compliance (reg 9); this is the evidence base if entitlement is challenged.
- **Carry-over:** 4 weeks of the 5.6 (the reg 13(1) EU-derived element) can carry over where the worker could not take it because of sick leave (18 months) or because the employer failed to recognise the right, encourage leave or warn of loss; the additional 1.6 weeks carries over only if a relevant agreement so provides.
- **Do not pay in lieu** of the 5.6 weeks except on termination (reg 13A(6) and reg 14).
- **Enforcement:** Employment Tribunal claim for the reg 30 remedy; HSE/local authority for the wider WTR.

## Bottom line for the worker

Every worker in Great Britain is entitled by statute to **5.6 weeks'** paid annual leave per leave year, and that entitlement is capped at **28 days**, which is exactly what 5.6 weeks amounts to for a five-day-week worker.

answer:
## Scope

I read 'the original DNS specification' as RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 as originally published. The numeric wire-format limits are in RFC 1035. No implementation-specific or later-RFC limit is being reported.

## Answer

| Object | Maximum | What is counted |
|---|---:|---|
| Single label | 63 octets | Label data only; the length prefix is not part of the label. |
| Encoded label field | 64 octets | 1 length octet plus up to 63 data octets. |
| Full domain name | 255 octets | Uncompressed wire encoding: all label length octets, all label data octets, and the final zero octet for the root. |

A label is not 64 octets; 64 is the on-the-wire field size. The label length octet uses its low six bits, so its literal-label range is 0 through 63. The high-order two bits must be 00 for a literal label. A length of 0 is the root label and is used only as the terminating null label.

## Specification text

RFC 1035 Section 2.3.4 ('Size limits') lists:

- labels: 63 octets or less
- names: 255 octets or less

RFC 1035 Section 3.1 says:

> The high order two bits of every length octet must be zero, and the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less.

> The total length of a domain name (i.e., label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less.

RFC 4343 Section 3.1 corroborates the label bound:

> ASCII labels, with a length from zero to 63 octets ... (The ASCII label of length zero is reserved for use as the name of the root node of the name tree.)

## Counting formula and checks

For a name with n labels of data lengths L1 through Ln:

    wire length = sum(1 + Li) + 1 <= 255, with 0 <= Li <= 63

The final +1 is the zero length octet of the root.

- Maximum single label: L = 63 octets. Its encoded field is 64 octets. A one-label name is 1 + 63 + 1 = 65 octets, so the label bound binds before the name bound.
- Maximum name using 63-octet labels: three labels of 63 and one of 61: (1+63)*3 + (1+61) + 1 = 192 + 62 + 1 = 255 octets. The total label-data content is 3*63 + 61 = 250 octets. In presentation form this is 63.63.63.61, which is 253 characters without the trailing dot and 254 with it. The 255 figure is wire octets, not characters.
- Maximum number of labels: 127 one-octet labels: 127*(1+1) + 1 = 255 octets.
- Root name: one zero octet, 1 octet.

## Clarifications

- The 255 count includes the terminating root label's zero octet. Excluding it would give 254, which is not the specification's count.
- Compression pointers are two-octet pointers. They may make a name's representation in a message shorter, but they do not change the logical name. The 255-octet limit applies to the uncompressed name.
- Presentation-format length can exceed 253 characters when escaping is required, for example when dots or non-printable octets are escaped. The octet limit is on the wire encoding, not on escaped text.
- Some APIs or later guidance use a 253-character presentation limit. That is a presentation or implementation convention, not a different RFC 1035 wire limit.
- The label limit and name limit are independent: a label may be at most 63 octets, and a full name may be at most 255 octets.

## Final values

Label: 63 octets of label data, or 64 octets including the length octet.

Full domain name: 255 octets in uncompressed wire encoding, including all label length octets and the root terminator.

question: H8
answer:
ANSWER

US federal Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for PFOA in drinking water:

- As the rule lists it: 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) — the rule text also writes it as "4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)".
- In nanograms per litre: 4.0 ng/L (identical to 4.0 ppt for water; conversion factor is exactly 1, so no rounding is applied and the rule's two significant figures are preserved).

AUTHORITY AND CITATION

- Rule: PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR), final rule, 89 FR 32532 (page 32535 et seq.), published in the Federal Register on 26 April 2024 (FR Doc. 2024-07773), issued under the Safe Drinking Water Act.
- Verbatim from the rule's preamble/regulatory summary: "the EPA is promulgating individual Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for PFOA and PFOS at 4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)."
- Verbatim from EPA's summary table for the same rule: "PFOA — Final MCLG: Zero — Final MCL (enforceable levels): 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)."
- Codification: the MCLs are promulgated as amendments to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations at 40 CFR part 141. Compliance is determined by running annual averages at the sampling point.

UNIT CONVERSION (shown, not assumed)

- 1 ppt = 1 part per 10^12 parts.
- For water, 1 L has a mass of about 1 kg = 10^12 ng (1 ng = 10^-9 g).
- Therefore 1 ppt ≈ 1 ng/L for aqueous samples, and 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L exactly, with no arithmetic change and no rounding.
- The rule itself supplies this equivalence ("ng/L or ppt"), so the ng/L figure is the rule's own expression, not an outside conversion.

WHAT THIS VALUE IS AND IS NOT

- It is an enforceable MCL, applying to community and non-transient non-community public water systems.
- It is not the MCLG. The MCLG for PFOA is zero (0) — a non-enforceable health goal. The enforceable MCL of 4.0 ng/L is set as close to that goal as is feasible.
- It is not the Hazard Index MCL. That is a separate, unitless limit of 1 applying to mixtures of two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS. PFOA is expressly excluded from the Hazard Index (PFOA and PFOS are regulated individually as likely carcinogens).
- It is not a combined PFOA+PFOS limit; the rule sets separate individual MCLs of 4.0 ng/L for each of PFOA and PFOS.
- It is a federal value. States may set limits no less strict than the NPDWR; stricter state limits are outside this answer.

STATUS CAVEAT FOR THE READER

The MCL value of 4.0 ng/L is as promulgated in the 2024 final rule (effective 26 June 2024, with MCL compliance obligations beginning in 2029). Compliance-deadline extensions or implementation adjustments do not alter the promulgated MCL number, but because the rule has been subject to subsequent administrative and judicial activity, anyone relying on this for enforcement purposes should confirm current status against EPA's PFAS NPDWR page and the Federal Register docket (EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0114) at the time of use. Nothing in the sourced rule text supports any value other than 4.0 ng/L (4.0 ppt) for PFOA.

question: H12
answer:
ANSWERS (Texas Instruments LM317, base/LM317A/LM317M versions)

| # | Ask | Value | Unit | Where it comes from |
|---|-----|-------|------|---------------------|
| 1 | Absolute maximum input-to-output voltage differential, V_I − V_O | 40 | V | Absolute Maximum Ratings table, row 'V_I − V_O Input-to-output differential voltage', MAX column |
| 2 | Typical reference voltage, V_REF | 1.25 | V | Electrical Characteristics table, V_REF 'Reference voltage', TYP column |

1. ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM INPUT-TO-OUTPUT VOLTAGE DIFFERENTIAL = 40 V

Datasheet text as printed (TI LM317M, SLVS297P – April 2000, revised March 2014, Section 6.1):

  'Absolute Maximum Ratings(1) over operating temperature range (unless otherwise noted)
   V_I − V_O  Input-to-output differential voltage   MAX 40 V
   T_J        Operating virtual junction temperature  MAX 150 °C
   (1) Stresses beyond those listed under "absolute maximum ratings" may cause permanent damage to the device.
       These are stress ratings only, and functional operation of the device at these or any other conditions beyond
       those indicated under "recommended operating conditions" is not implied. Exposure to absolute-maximum-rated
       conditions for extended periods may affect device reliability.'

The same 40 V figure is the rating for the standard 1.5 A LM317 and for the LM317A (40 V) in their respective TI datasheets. It is the differential (input minus output) that is rated, not the absolute input voltage relative to ground — the regulator is a floating topology and 'detects only the input-to-output differential voltage' (TI product page), which is why the part can regulate supplies far above 40 V as long as the differential stays under 40 V.

Variant map — do not apply 40 V blindly across the family:

| Device | Max input-to-output differential | Max output voltage | Rated output current |
|---|---|---|---|
| LM317 (standard, SLVS044) | 40 V | 37 V | 1.5 A |
| LM317A (high accuracy) | 40 V | 37 V | 1.5 A |
| LM317M (SLVS297P) | 40 V | 37 V | 0.5 A |
| LM317L (low current) | 40 V | 32 V (typ. family limit) | 0.1 A |
| LM317HV | 60 V | 57 V | 1.5 A |

The 60 V value belongs only to the LM317HV ordering option; it is not a relaxation of the LM317/LM317A rating. If a design needs more than 40 V differential, the LM317HV must be specified explicitly by full orderable part number.

Engineering notes that must travel with this number:
- 40 V is a stress rating, not an operating point. Continuous operation is bounded by the Recommended Operating Conditions (input-to-output differential 3 V minimum for regulation, 40 V maximum) and by thermal limits (T_J ≤ 125 °C recommended, 150 °C absolute), not by the absolute-maximum number alone.
- Because only the differential is rated, a short circuit on the output of a high-voltage-input design drives the differential to the full input voltage and destroys the part. The datasheet states this directly: 'avoid short-circuiting the output.' Any design where V_IN can exceed 40 V with the output pulled to ground needs either an LM317HV, a clamp, or output short-circuit protection external to the regulator.
- Output-voltage programming is limited to 37 V (LM317/LM317A) for the same reason: at V_OUT = 37 V the input may sit at 40 V differential, i.e. up to ~77 V absolute, and the input-to-output capacitor/diode network must be rated for that.

2. TYPICAL REFERENCE VOLTAGE = 1.25 V

The reference is the ADJUST-to-OUTPUT differential the regulator forces across the program resistor R1, so the design equation is:

  V_OUT = V_REF × (1 + R2/R1) + I_ADJ × R2,  with V_REF = 1.25 V typical

Datasheet values (standard LM317/LM317A Electrical Characteristics, V_REF row, 3 V ≤ (V_I − V_O) ≤ 40 V, 10 mA ≤ I_O ≤ 500 mA, T_J = 25 °C unless otherwise noted):

| Parameter | Min | Typ | Max | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| V_REF, LM317 (standard) | 1.20 | 1.25 | 1.30 | V |
| V_REF, LM317A (high accuracy) | 1.238 | 1.25 | 1.262 | V |

The LM317M datasheet prints the same nominal in its detailed description and application schematic ('feedback voltage ... 1.25 V'; 'Vref=1.25V'; 'Any output voltage from 1.25 V to 37 V can be obtained by using two resistors').

Engineering notes that must travel with this number:
- 1.25 V is the TYPICAL. For a worst-case design use the min/max window (1.20/1.30 V for standard LM317, ±1 % for LM317A), not 1.25 V. A ±4 % reference spread on the standard part maps directly into ±4 % on V_OUT before resistor tolerance is added.
- The reference is temperature dependent (datasheet ripple/noise and reference curves show roughly a few tenths of a percent drift over −40 °C to +125 °C); the min/max window above is specified over the operating temperature range, which is why it is wider than a 25 °C-only spec would be.
- The reference is only guaranteed for I_O ≥ 10 mA (minimum load current). Below that the output can rise above the programmed value, because the device's bias current (up to ~10 mA) flows out of the OUTPUT pin and must be consumed by the load or the feedback divider. Choose R1 ≤ 240 Ω for the standard part so the divider alone sinks the minimum load.
- For 1.2 V-class operation, V_OUT can be programmed below the 1.25 V nominal down to the reference itself; below ~1.25 V the device is no longer regulating against the reference and behaviour is not specified.

SOURCE AND REVISION CONTROL

Primary source for both values: Texas Instruments LM317 family datasheets, Absolute Maximum Ratings and Electrical Characteristics tables (LM317M revision SLVS297P, April 2000 – revised March 2014, corroborated by the TI LM317 product page and the standard LM317/LM317A datasheet SLVS044). Both figures are stable across TI revisions of the LM317 — the 40 V differential and the 1.25 V typical reference have not changed — but the LM317HV (60 V) and LM317L (0.1 A) are separate datasheets with their own tables. Any BOM, test plan or review checklist citing these numbers should cite the full orderable part number plus datasheet literature number, e.g. 'LM317DCYR, SLVS044 rev X, V_I−V_O abs max 40 V; V_REF 1.25 V typ', so the value cannot be silently inherited by an LM317HV or third-party LM317 clone whose absolute-maximum table differs.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THESE ANSWERS
- Substituting LM317HV → ask 1 becomes 60 V.
- Substituting LM317A → ask 2 typical stays 1.25 V but the min/max window tightens to 1.238/1.262 V.
- A non-TI (second-source) LM317 → re-read that vendor's Absolute Maximum Ratings; the reference typical is nominally the same 1.25 V but the guaranteed window and test currents can differ.
Neither change is present in the stated request, which asks for the TI LM317 values, so the reported values stand at 40 V and 1.25 V.

question: H14
answer:
REGULATORY ANALYSIS — 14 CFR § 91.151 FUEL RESERVE APPLICABILITY TO GLIDERS

1. ANSWER
A glider is not subject to any fuel reserve under 14 CFR § 91.151. The required reserve to begin a VFR flight in a glider is ZERO minutes — i.e., no regulatory fuel reserve exists, because § 91.151 imposes its reserve only on airplans and rottercraft, and a glider is neither.

Any answer of "30 minutes by day / 45 minutes by night" applied to a glider is a miscitation of § 91.151(a). Those figures govern airplans only.

2. GOVERING TEXT (as fetched from eCFR, 14 CFR 91.151, current)
"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplan under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rottercraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Three features of the text control the answer:
(a) Each paragraph is limited by aircraft category: "an airplan" in (a), "a rottercraft" in (b).
(b) There is no residual paragraph such as "any other aircraft." The section simply stops after (b).
(c) The reserve is expressed in minutes of fuel at normal cruising speed — a concept that has no referent in an aircraft without a fuel-burning powerplant.

3. WHY A GLIDER IS OUTSIDE THE RULE — DEFINITIONS (14 CFR 1.1)
- Airplan: "an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft heavier than air."
- Glider: "a heavier-than-air aircraft that is supported in flight by dynamic reaction against the air and that does not depend principally on a powerplant for forward motion."
- Rottercraft: a heavier-than-air aircraft that depends principally on one or more rotors for support in flight.

A glider satisfies neither the airplan nor the rottercraft definition: it is not engine-driven (in the certification sense) and it is not rotor-supported. § 91.151 therefore has no operative clause that reaches it. The result is not an exception, waiver, or ambiguity — it is simple non-applicability.

4. THE MOTORGLIDER QUESTION (self-launching and sustainer-powered gliders)
Applicability turns on the aircraft's regulatory category, not on whether an engine happens to be bolted on.
- Self-launching and sustainer motorgliders are ordinarily type-certificated and airworthiness-certificated in the GLIDER category. They remain gliders, and § 91.151 does not apply. Reserve = 0 minutes regulatorily.
- If, exceptionally, a particular aircraft is certificated in the AIRPLANE category, it is an airplan for § 91.151 purposes and the (a) reserve applies: 30 minutes by day, 45 minutes at night, after reaching the first point of intended landing.
- Independently of § 91.151, any fuel or endurance limitation printed in the FAA-approved flight manual for a powered glider is an operating limitation binding on the pilot. That is an aircraft limitation, not a § 91.151 reserve, and it should not be reported as one.

5. WHAT THE SECTION DOES NOT SAY (COMMON MISREADINGS TO CORRECT)
- § 91.151 contains NO alternate-airport fuel requirement. The "to the destination, then to the alternate, then reserve" construction belongs to the IFR fuel rule (§ 91.167), not to § 91.151 and not to this question, which is expressly VFR.
- § 91.151 does not create a generic "all aircraft" reserve that a glider pilot must somehow satisfy with ballast, altitude, or time aloft.
- No state or local rule supplies a fuel reserve for gliders; the field is occupied by the federal rule and the answer does not vary by state.
- Nothing in § 91.151 relieves a glider pilot of the remaining subpart B obligations (weather minimums, airspace, airworthiness, operating limitations). Those are separate rules; they are simply not fuel-reserve rules.

6. APPLICABILITY TABLE
| Aircraft category | Governing paragraph | Reserve after first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| Airplan, VFR, day | § 91.151(a)(1) | 30 minutes |
| Airplan, VFR, night | § 91.151(a)(2) | 45 minutes |
| Rottercraft, VFR | § 91.151(b) | 20 minutes |
| Glider (incl. motorglider certificated in the glider category), VFR | none | 0 minutes — no § 91.151 reserve |

7. PRACTICAL FLIGHT-PLANNING NOTE (NOT REGULATORY)
ZERO regulatory reserve is a floor set by the rule, not a flight-planning recommendation. Glider pilots manage energy rather than fuel, and prudent practice — club standards, competition rules, and instructor guidance — typically calls for arrival at the destination with a usable altitude/thermal margin sufficient to reach a landable field. A motorglider pilot who intends to use the engine should flight-plan against the manual's endurance figures and, as good practice, the airplane 30/45-minute standard, understanding that this is voluntary prudence (or a manual limitation) and not a § 91.151 obligation.

8. CITATIONS
- 14 CFR § 91.151 (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions) — eCFR, current, verified text.
- 14 CFR § 1.1 (definitions of airplan, glider, rottercraft).
- 14 CFR § 91.167 (IFR fuel requirements) — cited only to show the alternate-fuel construct is not in § 91.151.

question: H16
answer:
ANSWER (US federal default): A property-carrying interstate truck driver subject to FMCSA hours-of-service rules may drive up to 8 cumulative hours of driving time before a break is required. At that point the driver must take at least 30 consecutive minutes of non-driving time before driving again.

Governing rule: 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii); FMCSA HOS Visor Card (property-carrying drivers). The rule is a 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving time without at least a 30-minute interruption. It is measured by cumulative driving time, not by elapsed on-duty time and not by 8 consecutive hours of driving.

Qualifying break: any non-driving period of at least 30 consecutive minutes. It may be off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty not driving, or any consecutive combination of those. The break need not be off-duty.

What the break does and does not do:
- It resets the 8-hour break clock.
- It does not reset the 11-hour daily driving limit or the 14-hour driving window. Only 10 consecutive hours off duty resets those.
- The separate property-carrying limits remain: maximum 11 hours driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty; no driving beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty; and the 60/70-hour limit over 7/8 consecutive days, with a 34-hour restart available.

Scope and caveats:
- This 8-hour figure is for US federal property-carrying CMV operations. Passenger-carrying rules differ; the FMCSA visor card describes the 30-minute break requirement as property-carrier only. Passenger carriers should verify 49 CFR 395.5, including the 10-hour driving limit after 8 consecutive hours off duty and the 15-hour on-duty limit.
- Exemptions and exceptions must be checked for the specific operation: short-haul 150 air-mile/14-hour exception, adverse driving conditions, agricultural exceptions, state intrastate rules, and any active emergency waiver. Adverse driving conditions can extend the 11/14 limits by up to 2 hours but do not eliminate the 30-minute break requirement.
- If the operation is in the EU rather than the US: Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 Article 7 requires a break of at least 45 minutes after 4.5 hours of driving; the break may be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes. EU daily driving is normally 9 hours, extendable to 10 hours twice a week, with 56 hours weekly and 90 hours fortnightly.

Compliance procedure:
1. Confirm applicability: interstate commerce, CMV definition, property-carrying versus passenger-carrying, and any exemption.
2. Track cumulative driving time since the last qualifying 30-minute non-driving interruption.
3. At 8 cumulative hours of driving, prohibit further driving until a 30-consecutive-minute non-driving period is recorded.
4. Record the break as off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty not driving, or a consecutive combination; the period must be uninterrupted for at least 30 minutes.
5. Audit ELD records for 8-hour-break violations, and separately for 11-hour, 14-hour, and 60/70-hour violations. Do not treat the 30-minute break as a reset of the 11-hour or 14-hour clocks.

question: H1
answer:
# Minimum rest between duty days for a US airline flight attendant

## Answer

**10 consecutive hours**, for a US Part 121 air carrier operating domestic, flag, or supplemental operations, when the flight attendant's scheduled duty period was 14 hours or less. This is a floor: 14 CFR 121.467(b)(3) states the rest period "may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours."

If the scheduled duty period was **more than 14 hours but not more than 20 hours**, the required rest is **12 consecutive hours**, which may be reduced to **10 consecutive hours** only if the flight attendant is then given a subsequent rest period of at least **14 consecutive hours** beginning no later than **24 hours** after the start of the reduced rest (121.467(b)(7)–(8)).

## Part 121 (§ 121.467) rest table — domestic, flag, supplemental

| Scheduled duty period | Required scheduled rest between duty periods | Reduction permitted |
|---|---|---|
| 14 h or less | **10 consecutive hours** | None — cannot go below 10 (b)(3) |
| More than 14 h, up to 20 h (augmented/extra-flight-attendant provisions of (b)(4)–(b)(6)) | **12 consecutive hours** | To 10 h, only with a subsequent 14 h rest starting ≤24 h after the reduced rest began (b)(8) |

Supporting definitions in 121.467(a):

- **Duty period** — "the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder." The rest clock therefore starts at **release**, not at block-in or at the last flight's arrival. Debrief, post-flight paperwork, and any other task before release extend the duty period and push the start of rest later.
- **Rest period** — "the period free of all restraint or duty ... and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." A rest period during which the carrier requires the flight attendant to remain reachable and respond (e.g., certain reserve or phone-contact obligations) is exposed to challenge as not rest.
- **Flight attendant** — cabin crew assigned to duty in an aircraft during flight time, other than a flight crewmember.

## Worked example

Duty period ends (release) at 21:30 local, duty period was 12.5 h → 10 h rest required → earliest permissible report for the next duty period is 07:30 local the following day. If that same duty period had been 15 h (say release at 23:00), 12 h rest would be required → earliest report 11:00, unless the carrier uses the (b)(8) reduction to 10 h, in which case report at 09:00 is permissible but a 14 h rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 23:00 the following day (24 h after the 23:00 start of the reduced rest).

## Which rule applies — the distinctions that change the number

The number is not the same across all US operators, so state the premise explicitly:

| Operator / rule | Rest after a ≤14 h duty period | Reduction | Rest after a >14 h duty period |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Part 121** domestic/flag/supplemental — § 121.467 | **10 h** | Not below 10 h | **12 h** (duty ≤20 h) |
| **Part 135** — § 135.273(b)(2)–(3) | **9 h** | To **8 h** with a subsequent 10 h rest beginning ≤24 h later | 12 h, reducible to 10 h with 14 h make-up (135.273(b)(7)–(8)) |
| **Part 91 subpart K** — § 91.1062(a)(2)–(3) | **9 h** | To **8 h** with a subsequent 10 h rest beginning ≤24 h later | 12 h, reducible to 10 h with 14 h make-up |

For a scheduled airline (Part 121), the answer is **10 hours**. The 9-hour/8-hour figures are the Part 135 and Part 91K numbers and should not be applied to a Part 121 carrier.

## Discrepancy to flag, not to average

The FAA's public FAQ page "What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?" states that in most cases "you must have at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest," reducible to eight. That text is consistent with §§ 135.273 and 91.1062 but **inconsistent with the current § 121.467 text**, which requires 10 hours and forbids reduction below 10. Where a secondary source and the codified regulation disagree, the regulation governs; do not split the difference or report 9 hours for a Part 121 carrier. If a questioner is relying on the FAQ, the correct response is to point to § 121.467(b)(2)–(3).

## Scope and caveats

- **Part 117 does not apply to flight attendants.** Part 117 flight time/duty/rest limits cover flightcrew members (pilots). Flight attendant duty and rest are governed by § 121.467.
- **Collective bargaining agreements and company policy can be stricter.** The regulation is a legal minimum; a CBA or ops manual may impose longer rest. Where they conflict, the more restrictive provision governs in practice. Verify the applicable CBA before advising a specific crew member.
- **Reserve and airport standby** are not resolved by § 121.467 itself; whether such time is duty (and therefore when the rest clock starts) generally depends on the CBA and the carrier's operations specifications. Treat as a contract question, not a regulatory one.
- **Deadhead/positioning** is duty, not rest; it sits inside the duty period.
- **International/foreign operations** can attract additional or different requirements (e.g., foreign authority rules); § 121.467 is the US baseline only.
- **Pending rulemaking:** a rulemaking docket exists (FAA-2019-0770) touching flight attendant duty/rest. The current codified text quoted above remains the 10-hour/12-hour standard; confirm no final rule has issued before relying on this in a compliance document.

## Compliance check to apply

1. Classify the operation (Part 121 domestic/flag/supplemental vs. 135 vs. 91K) — this selects 10 h vs. 9 h.
2. Measure the **scheduled** duty period from report to release; determine whether it exceeds 14 h (and whether it exceeds 20 h, which is not permitted under (b)(1) absent the (b)(4)–(b)(6) conditions).
3. Assign 10 h (≤14 h duty) or 12 h (>14 h duty) of rest between release and the next report.
4. If reducing 12 h to 10 h under (b)(8), schedule the 14 h make-up rest to begin no later than 24 h after the reduced rest began, and do not schedule a duty period over 14 h in that 24-hour window.
5. Confirm the rest is free of all restraint or duty, and check the CBA for any longer requirement.

The first reads: "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."

ANSWER

A drone counts as a 'small unmanned aircraft' / 'small UAS' under FAA rules only if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS ON TAKEOFF, INCLUDING EVERYTHING THAT IS ON BOARD OR OTHERWISE ATTACHED TO THE AIRCRAFT.

- Governing text: 14 CFR § 107.3 (definitions), applicable via 14 CFR part 107 ('Small unmanned aircraft system').
- Literal limit: < 55 lb. 55.0 lb exactly is NOT small; 54.9 lb is.
- Metric equivalent: 55 lb = 24.9476 kg (exactly 24.94758035 kg at 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg). Because the limit is strict, use 24.94 kg as the practical metric ceiling — 24.95 kg already equals ~55.006 lb and would fall outside the definition.

1. CONTROLING REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim)

14 CFR § 107.3, Definitions (identical in eCFR current text and the 2026 edition PDF of 14 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 107):

  'Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'

  'Small unmanned aircraft system (small UAS) means a small unmanned aircraft and its associated elements (including communication links and the components that control the small unmanned aircraft) that are required for the safe and efficient operation of the small unmanned aircraft in the national airspace system.'

Corroborating FAA statement (FAA newsroom, 'Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Regulations (Part 107)'): the part 107 rules 'cover a broad spectrum of commercial and government uses for drones weighing less than 55 pounds'; and for carriage of property for compensation or hire, the drone 'including its attached systems, payload, and cargo, weighs less than 55 pounds total.'

Corroboration from the other direction (FAA Aeronautical Information Manual, AIM 11-2-2 and the AIM table of contents): 'Large UAS (MGOW 55 Pounds or More)' is a separate category, and 'UAS weighing 55 pounds MGOW or more must be registered under 14 CFR part 47 ... while UAS less than 55 pounds may be registered under the FAAA's newer 14 CFR part 48 online system.' The 55-lb line is therefore the boundary in both directions: below = small, at or above = not small.

2. WHAT THE WEIGHT INCLUDES

The definition is takeoff weight, not airframe weight. Count:
  - airframe, motors, propellers, ESCs, flight controller, batteries;
  - cameras, gimbals, antennas, transpoders/ADS-B units if fitted;
  - any payload, cargo, slung load, dispensing device, or attachment;
  - anything 'otherwise attached' at the moment of takeoff.
Excluded: the ground-side control station / transmitter and other associated elements of the 'system' that are not on board or attached to the aircraft (those are part of the 'small UAS' but not part of the aircraft's weight). Note this is the only place the aircraft/system distinction changes the number, and it changes it in the operator's favour only for ground-side equipment.

Practical consequence: a drone whose empty weight is, say, 52 lb with a 4-lb camera and gimbal is 56 lb on takeoff and is NOT a small unmanned aircraft, even though its 'airframe' is under the line.

3. ADJACENT THRESHOLDS — DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 'SMALL' DEFINITION

  | Threshold | Value | What it governs | Does it define 'small'? |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Small unmanned aircraft (Part 107 § 107.3) | < 55 lb (24.9476 kg) | The definition itself; eligibility for part 107 | YES — this is the answer |
  | Category 1 operations over people (§ 107.110) | <= 0.55 lb (249.5 g) on takeoff and throughout the operation, no exposed lacerating rotating parts | Sustained flight over open-air assemblies without further showing | NO — a sub-category inside 'small' |
  | Category 2 / 3 operations over people (§§ 107.115–107.130) | No weight number; kinetic-energy-based, declared compliance + labeling | Operations over people | NO — still requires a small unmanned aircraft (< 55 lb) |
  | Category 4 (§ 107.140) | Airworthiness certificate, operating rules of part 91 | Operations over people | NO — still requires a small unmanned aircraft |
  | Recreational registration (49 U.S.C. 44809 / AIM 11-2-1) | > 0.55 lb must register | Registration only | NO |
  | Part 107 registration | All weights, no minimum | Registration only | NO |
  | Part 47 registration / 'Large UAS' | >= 55 lb MGOW | Registration path, not part 107 | Confirms the 55-lb line |

4. EDGE CASES AND COMMON ERORS

  a) 'Exactly 55 lb.' Not small. The rule says 'less than.' Build, load, and document to a margin (e.g., target <= 54.5 lb / 24.7 kg) so that scale tolerance, dirt, tape, and post-build additions don't push you over.
  b) 'Can I get a waiver to fly a 60-lb drone under part 107?' No. § 107.205 waivers apply to listed operating rules (e.g., beyond visual line of sight, 400-ft ceiling, over-people operations), not to the § 107.3 definition. A heavier aircraft must go a different regulatory route — e.g., a § 44807 exemption, part 91 operations with an airworthiness certificate, or public-aircraft authority — and is then not a 'small UAS.'
  c) 'My drone is 55 lb with the battery but 54 lb without.' Irrelevant: the battery is on board at takeoff.
  d) 'The transmitter and tablet push it over.' Those are ground-side associated elements, not attached to the aircraft; they don't count toward the 55 lb. A tablet mounted on the controller that is itself attached to the aircraft would count.
  e) 'I'm flying recreationally, so a higher limit applies.' No. The recreational pathway does not raise the 55-lb small-aircraft line; it changes which set of operating rules and which registration path applies.
  f) 'I'm outside the U.S.' This answer is F.A.A.-specific (14 CFR part 107). Other jurisdictions set their own lines and this answer must not be carried over.

5. HOW TO VERIFY AT TIME OF USE (rules change)

  1. Open eCFR: 14 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 107, § 107.3, and read the 'Small unmanned aircraft' definition. Alternatively the GovInfo annual edition PDF of 14 CFR part 107.
  2. Confirm the phrase is 'less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached.' If the number or the inclusive/exclusive wording differs, the answer changes and the new text controls.
  3. Cross-check the AIM UAS chapter's 'Large UAS (MGOW 55 Pounds or More)' entry — it should still put the line at 55 lb.
  4. Confirm the aircraft is being flown under part 107 rather than part 91/exemption/public aircraft, since those routes can allow heavier aircraft but do not make them 'small.'

BOTTOM LINE: 55 lb (24.9476 kg) — and strictly under it.

answer:
BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL (U.S., 14 CFR 91.155)

ANSWER

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Flight visibility | 3 statute miles |
| Distance from clouds — below | 500 feet |
| Distance from clouds — above | 1,000 feet |
| Distance from clouds — horizontal | 2,000 feet |

Authority: 14 CFR 91.155(a), table row "Class E: Less than 10,000 feet MSL." Identical figures appear in the FAA AIM/AIP (TBL ENR 1.4-1) and the GPO CFR text.

1. SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY
- Applies to all aircraft operating under VFR in Class E airspace at any altitude below 10,000 ft MSL.
- Class E has NO day/night distinction and NO helicopter/airplane distinction for these minima. The single row above covers day and night, all aircraft categories.
- "Flight visibility" is the visibility observed from the cockpit in flight (91.155(a)), not reported ground visibility. Ground visibility enters only through 91.155(d) below.
- "Distance from clouds" is a three-part requirement that must be satisfied simultaneously: at least 500 ft below any cloud, at least 1,000 ft above any cloud, and at least 2,000 ft horizontally from any cloud.

2. CRITICAL BOUNDARY — DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 10,000 FT ROW
Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL is a different row: 5 statute miles visibility; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 statute mile horizontal. The 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 figures are valid only strictly below 10,000 ft MSL. Because 91.155(e) provides that an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E area is considered within the airspace directly below that area, an aircraft at exactly the floor of a Class E layer takes the minima of the airspace beneath — relevant to floors at 10,000 ft and at 1,200 ft AGL/700 ft AGL.

3. CORRECTION TO A COMMON MISCONCEPTION (sub-band split inside Class E)
There is no 1,200 ft AGL sub-band inside Class E. The 1,200 ft AGL threshold appears only in the Class G rows of the table. Class E airspace is often floored at 1,200 ft AGL (or 700 ft AGL, or the surface), but once you are inside Class E the minima above are the same at 1,300 ft AGL as at 9,900 ft MSL. The figures that do change across altitude bands and day/night are the Class G figures: below 1,200 ft AGL day, 1 SM / clear of clouds (airplanes), 1/2 SM / clear of clouds (helicopters); above 1,200 ft AGL but below 10,000 ft MSL, day 1 SM with 500/1,000/2,000, night 3 SM with 500/1,000/2,000. Do not apply Class G visibility to Class E: the cloud clearances happen to match, but the visibility does not (1 SM vs 3 SM).

4. ADJACENT REQUIREMENTS THAT BIND THE SAME FLIGHT
- 91.155(c): within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport (including a Class E surface area), no VFR flight beneath the ceiling when the ceiling is below 1,000 ft. A Class E surface area with a 900 ft ceiling therefore blocks VFR even though the visibility/cloud-clearance row is met.
- 91.155(d): to take off, land, or enter the traffic pattern of an airport within the surface area of Class B/C/D/E airspace designated for that airport, ground visibility must be at least 3 statute miles; if ground visibility is not reported, flight visibility must be at least 3 statute miles.
- 91.157: Special VFR is the only relief from 91.155(c) and (d); it requires an ATC clearance and, at night, an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped aircraft.
- The traffic-pattern exceptions in 91.155(b) (helicopter clear of clouds at 1/2 SM; airplane clear of clouds at 1-3 SM at night) apply ONLY in Class G airspace below 1,200 ft AGL. They do not create Class E exceptions.

5. UNIT CONVERSIONS (secondary reference only; the rule is written in statute miles and feet)
- 3 statute miles = 4.83 km = 2.61 NM
- 500 ft = 152 m; 1,000 ft = 305 m; 2,000 ft = 610 m

6. VERIFICATION AGAINST SOURCE TEXT
Every quoted source (eCFR Part 91, FAA 91.155 PDF, GPO CFR-2022 sec. 91-155, FAA AIM ENR 1.4) states for Class E less than 10,000 ft MSL: "3 statute miles; 500 feet below; 1,000 feet above; 2,000 feet horizontal." All four also state for Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL: "5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below; 1,000 feet above; 1 statute mile horizontal." No source assigns a day/night or helicopter split to Class E. The figures in the answer table, in the boundary note, and in the conversion line are mutually consistent; the 3 SM value is strictly less than the 5 SM boundary-row value, and the 500 ft below figure is strictly less than the 1,000 ft above figure as written in the rule.

7. IF ANOTHER JURISDICTION APPLIES
These numbers are U.S. FAA values. ICAO/EASA-style regimes define Class E minima differently (commonly 5 km visibility and 1,000 ft vertical / 1.5 km horizontal in some states), so the jurisdiction must be confirmed before these figures are used outside U.S.-registered operations in U.S. airspace.
