question: H14
answer:
ANSWER

Under 14 CFR § 91.151, a glider must carry no fuel reserve at all to begin a flight under VFR. Zero minutes. The section does not apply to gliders.

§ 91.151 is written in aircraft-category terms. Subsection (a) reaches only "a flight in an airplane"; subsection (b) reaches only "a flight in a rotorcraft." There is no residual clause covering aircraft generally. A glider is neither category, so no fuel-reserve minimum under § 91.151 attaches to it. The practical restatement: a pure (unpowered) glider has no fuel system and therefore no "fuel reserve" in any regulatory sense, and the regulation that would otherwise supply a number simply does not reach it.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, current eCFR, fetched 2026-11-17; identical in the 2025 and 2026 CFR print volumes)

"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.

(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—

(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or

(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Sources checked, all in agreement:
- eCFR current, 14 CFR 91.151 (sha256 a8a7e00944fb)
- GovInfo, CFR 2026 title 14 vol. 2, sec. 91.151 (sha256 25216af9b686)
- GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 14 vol. 2, sec. 91.151 XML (sha256 7c3230319ff7)
- eCFR Part 91 subpart B listing (sha256 50b3b0bc67a4), which shows § 91.151 sitting between "§§ 91.148-91.149 [Reserved]" and § 91.153

Because the three vintages are textually identical, the answer does not vary with the edition of § 91.151 chosen.

2. WHY A GLIDER IS OUTSIDE THE SECTION

(a) Plain text. The section is not written to "aircraft." It names two categories and stops. Where the drafters of Part 91 meant all aircraft they said so — compare § 91.7 ("No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is in an airworthy condition"), § 91.9, § 91.103, § 91.155. The category limitation in § 91.151 is therefore deliberate, not a drafting accident.

(b) Part 1.1 category definitions (14 CFR 1.1):
- Airplane: "an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft heavier than air, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its wings." The word "engine-driven" is definitional. A glider is not engine-driven in the sense that defines the category.
- Rotorcraft: "a heavier-than-air aircraft that depends principally for its support in flight on the lift generated by one or more rotors." A glider does not.
- Glider: "a heavier-than-air aircraft, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its lifting surfaces and whose free flight does not depend principally on an engine." This is a separate category, and it is the one a glider is certificated in.

(c) Consequence. A glider falls in neither (a) nor (b) of § 91.151. No number in the section is owed. The answer is 0 minutes.

3. DECISION TABLE — WHICH RESERVE APPLIES, BY CERTIFICATED CATEGORY

| Aircraft's airworthiness certificate category | Governing paragraph | Day VFR reserve after the first point of intended landing | Night VFR reserve after that point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glider (including self-launching and sustainer-equipped motor gliders certificated in the glider category) | none — § 91.151 does not apply | 0 minutes | 0 minutes |
| Airplane (including a motor glider certificated in the airplane category) | § 91.151(a) | 30 minutes at normal cruising speed | 45 minutes at normal cruising speed |
| Rotorcraft | § 91.151(b) | 20 minutes at normal cruising speed | 20 minutes at normal cruising speed |

How to determine which row applies: read the aircraft's airworthiness certificate and registration. The category stated there controls, not the marketing name on the fuselage. "Motor glider," "touring motor glider," "self-launcher," and "sustainer" are descriptive terms; the certificate says glider or airplane. A glider with a retractable engine that is certificated in the glider category stays in row 1 — the presence of a fuel tank does not convert it into an airplane for § 91.151 purposes. Conversely, a touring motor glider certificated in the airplane category is in row 2 and owes 30/45 minutes even when the engine is used only for launch.

4. WORKED APPLICATION FOR THE AIRPLANE-CATEGORY BRANCH (row 2), SO THE BOUNDARY IS NUMERICALLY EXPLICIT

Assume a motor glider certificated in the airplane category, normal cruising speed 100 kt, day VFR, first point of intended landing 120 nm away.
- Fuel to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast conditions: 120 nm at the forecast groundspeed. With a 10 kt headwind, groundspeed 90 kt, so 120/90 = 1.33 h = 80 minutes of fuel.
- Reserve after that point, day: 30 minutes at normal cruising speed = 0.5 h x 100 kt = 50 nm equivalent.
- Total minimum at brake release: 80 + 30 = 110 minutes of fuel.
- Same flight at night: reserve 45 minutes = 0.75 h x 100 kt = 75 nm equivalent; total 80 + 45 = 125 minutes.
Note the two different speed bases the regulation itself uses: distance to the first landing point is flown at expected groundspeed (wind included), while the reserve is computed "assuming normal cruising speed" (no wind credit).

5. WHAT STILL CONSTRAINS A GLIDER PILOT, GIVEN § 91.151 DOES NOT

The absence of a § 91.151 reserve is not an absence of obligation. A complete answer for a pilot or a compliance document should note:
- § 91.3(a): the pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft.
- § 91.103: before beginning a flight the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight; for a flight not in the vicinity of an airport that information includes fuel requirements and alternatives available. For a glider this maps onto launch/soaring/altitude and off-field landing planning rather than fuel quantity.
- § 91.9(a): the aircraft must be operated in compliance with its approved flight manual, markings, and placards (for gliders, the FAA-approved flight manual and operating limitations). Where a manufacturer's manual or an operating limitation sets a limitation, that limitation binds independently of § 91.151.
- § 91.13(a): no person may operate an aircraft in a careless or reckless manner so as to endanger life or property.
- § 91.155: VFR weather minimums still apply to gliders in full.
- § 91.153 (VFR flight plan information) and § 91.155 are the neighboring VFR provisions; § 91.153 is procedural and does not create a fuel reserve.
- For IFR, § 91.167 governs — but gliders are not flown IFR under Part 91, and § 91.167 is outside this question.

6. SCOPE AND CAVEATS
- Jurisdiction: U.S. FAA rules under 14 CFR. If the operation is under EASA or another authority, this answer does not carry over; EASA's SERA/NCO fuel rules are drafted differently and must be checked separately.
- Aircraft meaning: "glider" here means an aircraft certificated in the glider category. The only realistic way the number changes is the airplane-category motor glider branch in section 3 above.
- Interpretive material: this answer rests on the regulatory text, which is dispositive on its face. No FAA legal interpretation was available in the source set consulted, and none is needed to reach the result; if a legal interpretation is later required for a compliance filing, search the FAA legal interpretation database for § 91.151 before relying on this in a formal opinion.
- Verification step before use: (i) confirm the aircraft's certificate category; (ii) confirm § 91.151 has not been amended after the 2026 CFR volume by checking eCFR currency at the time of use.

question: H16
answer:
# How long a truck driver may drive before a mandatory break

## Headline answer

**8 hours of cumulative driving.** Under US federal Hours of Service rules (FMCSA), a property-carrying commercial driver must take a **30-minute break** once they have **driven for 8 cumulative hours without at least a 30-minute interruption**. This is the maximum continuous driving stretch before a break is legally required.

Jurisdiction matters: under **EU Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Article 7**, the equivalent figure is **4.5 hours of driving**, followed by an **uninterrupted break of at least 45 minutes**. If the driver operates under EU rules, the answer is 4.5 hours, not 8.

## Scoping statement (state this wherever the number is used)

The 8-hour figure applies to:

- **Jurisdiction:** United States, federal FMCSA Hours of Service (49 CFR Part 395), as amended effective 29 September 2020.
- **Vehicle/driver class:** property-carrying commercial motor vehicle (the 30-minute break requirement applies to property carriers; the visor card text states it is 'for property carriers only').
- **Break type:** the in-shift mandatory rest break during the driving day — not the end-of-shift daily rest period, and not the 11-hour or 60/70-hour driving limits.

If any of these is wrong, use the corresponding figure from the tables below instead.

## The rule, precisely

| Element | Requirement (property-carrying, US) |
|---|---|
| Trigger | 8 cumulative hours of driving since the last qualifying interruption |
| Required break | 30 consecutive minutes |
| What counts as the break | Any non-driving period of 30 consecutive minutes: on-duty not driving, off-duty, sleeper berth, or any consecutive combination of these |
| What it is not | Not a requirement to stop at exactly 8:00 — the driver may break earlier; the break must occur before exceeding 8 cumulative driving hours |

Note the word **cumulative**, not consecutive. Since the 2020 revision, short non-driving interruptions of less than 30 minutes do not reset the clock, but the 8 hours are counted cumulatively across the driving day rather than as one unbroken stretch.

## Related limits that are often confused with this one

These are separate constraints; the 8-hour break rule sits alongside them, not instead of them.

**Property-carrying (US)**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Driving limit after 10 consecutive hours off duty | 11 hours |
| Driving window | May not drive beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty; off-duty time does not extend it |
| On-duty cycle limit | 60 hours in 7 consecutive days / 70 hours in 8 consecutive days |
| Restart | 34 or more consecutive hours off duty resets the 7/8-day cycle |
| Sleeper berth split | Two periods, one at least 2 hours (in or out of berth) and the other at least 7 consecutive hours in the berth; pairing must total at least 10 hours; neither period counts against the 14-hour window when used together |
| Adverse driving conditions | May extend the 11-hour driving limit and 14-hour window by up to 2 hours (16-hour window for up to 13 hours of driving) |

**Passenger-carrying (US)** — for contrast; the 30-minute break rule does not apply here

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Driving limit after 8 consecutive hours off duty | 10 hours |
| On-duty limit | May not drive after 15 hours on duty; off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period |
| Cycle limit | 60/70 hours in 7/8 consecutive days |
| Sleeper berth split | Pairing must total at least 8 hours, neither period less than 2 hours |
| Adverse driving conditions | May extend the 10-hour driving limit and 15-hour on-duty limit by up to 2 hours |

**EU (Regulation 561/2006)**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Driving before a break (Art. 7) | 4.5 hours |
| Required break | 45 uninterpreted minutes (or 15 minutes + 30 minutes distributed across the 4.5-hour period) |
| Multi-manning break | 45 minutes may be taken in a moving vehicle driven by another driver, provided the resting driver does not assist with driving |
| Regular daily rest | At least 11 hours (may be split: first period at least 3 hours, second at least 9 hours) |
| Reduced daily rest | At least 9 hours but less than 11; at most 3 between any two weekly rests |
| Regular weekly rest | At least 45 hours |
| Reduced weekly rest | Less than 45 hours, may be shortened to at least 24 consecutive hours with equivalent compensation taken en bloc before the end of the third following week |

## Exceptions and edge cases to check before applying the 8-hour figure

1. **Short-haul exception.** A driver is exempt from the records-of-duty-status requirements if they operate within a **150 air-mile radius** of the normal work reporting location, report and return within **14 consecutive hours**, and do not exceed a **14-hour duty period**. Confirm whether the driver's operation qualifies before asserting the break rule as binding.
2. **Adverse driving conditions.** The 2-hour extension applies to the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window. It is not a licence to skip the 30-minute break; treat the break rule as still binding.
3. **Sleeper-berth pairing.** A qualifying sleeper-berth period can serve as the 30-minute interruption if it is at least 30 consecutive non-driving minutes, but the pairing rules for the 10-hour off-duty period are a separate analysis.
4. **Passenger-carrying operations.** The 30-minute break provision does not appear for passenger carriers; the binding constraint there is the 10-hour driving limit within a 15-hour on-duty period.
5. **Non-US operations.** Apply the EU figure (4.5 hours / 45 minutes) or the relevant national regime; do not mix the two numbers in one policy document.

## How to state it in a policy or dispatch document

> A property-carrying driver may not drive more than 8 cumulative hours without taking an interruption of at least 30 consecutive minutes. The interruption may be on-duty not driving, off-duty, sleeper berth, or any consecutive combination. This break is required in addition to the 11-hour driving limit, the 14-hour driving window, and the 60/70-hour cycle limit.

For an EU-operation policy, substitute: *a driver must take an uninterpreted break of at least 45 minutes after 4.5 hours of driving; the break may be replaced by 15 minutes followed by 30 minutes distributed across the driving period.*

## Sources relied on

- FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations* (property- and passenger-carrying driver tables, 30-minute driving break, 11-hour/14-hour limits, 60/70-hour limit, sleeper berth, adverse driving conditions).
- FMCSA, *Hours of Service Visor Card* (30-minute break — property carriers only; break satisfiable by any 30 consecutive non-driving minutes; 2020 revision effective 29 September 2020; short-haul exception; adverse driving conditions).
- Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Articles 7 and 8, and Article 4 definitions (f)-(j), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2020/1054.

question: H1
answer:
MINIMUM REST BETWEEN DUTY DAYS FOR A US FLIGHT ATTENDANT

ANSWER: 10 consecutive hours.

For a US airline operating under 14 CFR Part 121 (domestic, flag, or supplemental operations), a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next duty period. That 10 hours is a hard floor: the rule expressly prohibits reducing it below 10 consecutive hours under any circumstance, and the FAA declined requests to allow waivers or opt-outs.

Citation: 14 CFR 121.467(b)(2) and (b)(3), as amended by the FAA final rule "Flight Attendant Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements" (published October 4, 2022; effective 30 days after publication, i.e., early November 2022). Confirm the exact Federal Register citation and effective/compliance dates against the FR document before relying on them in a filing.

1. THE FULL TIERED SCHEME (do not quote the 10-hour figure alone)

| Scheduled duty period | Required scheduled rest before next duty period | Reducible? |
|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less | 10 consecutive hours | No. 121.467(b)(3) bars reduction below 10. |
| More than 14 hours, up to 20 hours (only as permitted by 121.467(b)(4)-(6), i.e., duty periods containing a qualifying mid-duty rest opportunity) | 12 consecutive hours | Yes, to 10 consecutive hours, but only if a subsequent rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest period (121.467(b)(8)). |
| Any 7 consecutive calendar days | At least 24 consecutive hours relieved of all further duty (121.467(b)(13)) | No. |

Key point for anyone reading only the headline number: the 12-hour tier still bottoms out at 10 hours. Nothing in Part 121 permits a flight attendant's between-duty rest to go below 10 consecutive hours. The pre-2022 rule (9 hours, reducible to 8) no longer exists for Part 121.

2. HOW THE 10 HOURS IS MEASURED

- Clock starts at completion of the scheduled duty period (release from the assignment) and stops at commencement of the subsequent duty period (report time). It is a continuous block, not an average and not a sum of fragments.
- "Rest period" is defined in 121.467(a) as a period free of all restraint or duty and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise. Airport standby, on-call availability, and any period in which the flight attendant is subject to call-back or duty restraint is not rest.
- The rule is written in terms of the scheduled rest period. Operationally, if delays or irregular operations would erode actual rest below 10 hours, the carrier cannot lawfully assign the next duty period as scheduled — the pairing must be delayed, reassigned, or the flight attendant released. Carriers manage this by building buffer between release and report. The FAA expressly declined to regulate company communications during rest; the only requirement it enforced is that the rest block be at least 10 consecutive hours.

3. SCOPE AND JURISDICTION — WHERE THE 10-HOUR ANSWER DOES NOT APPLY

The answer above is the Part 121 answer. The same question returns different numbers under other US regimes, and these are frequently confused:

- Part 135 (135.273(b)): 9 consecutive hours for a duty period of 14 hours or less, reducible to 8 if followed by a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest. This part was not raised to 10 by the 2022 rule.
- Part 91.1062 (program managers, e.g., certain fractional/private-program operations): 9 consecutive hours for a duty period of 14 hours or less, reducible to 8 with a 10-hour makeup rest on the same 24-hour trigger. Same 12-hour/10-hour structure for duty periods over 14 hours.
- Part 121 carriers may elect, under 121.467(c), to apply the Part 117 flightcrew duty and rest scheme to flight attendants instead, provided written procedures are established. Part 117 is structured differently (rest before a flight duty period, with limited reduction provisions). If a carrier has made this election, its operations specifications and manual govern, and the flat 10-hour answer should be verified against that election.
- Foreign carriers operating to/from the US are governed by their own state's rules plus applicable bilateral/Part 129 requirements; the FAA Part 121 flight-attendant rest rule does not set their crew rest.

If the requester's actual subject is a Part 135 operator, a Part 91 program, or a non-US carrier, the answer changes and should be re-run against that regime.

4. CONTRACTUAL LAYER (context, not the legal answer)

The regulatory figure is a floor. Collective bargaining agreements routinely set a higher scheduled-rest floor and separately define "actual rest" (commonly measured "behind the door" at the hotel). Example from a 2024 flight attendant agreement: scheduled rest of not less than 10 hours between duty periods, with actual rest per the FARs and a contractual minimum of 8 hours behind the door to absorb delays, plus a no-interruption clause allowing contact only within one hour of report. A carrier's CBA can therefore require more than 10 hours, but it can never lawfully require less.

5. SOURCE-HIERARCHY WARNING

The FAA's public FAQ page on flight attendant duty and rest requirements still states 9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8 — that page reflects the pre-2022 rule and is stale. The authoritative current text is the eCFR version of 121.467 (and the Federal Register final rule). Cite the CFR, not the FAQ, in any compliance document.

6. COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST (for applying this to a pairing or a manual)

1) Determine the scheduled duty period length for the preceding duty period.
2) If 14:00 or less: confirm at least 10:00 consecutive scheduled rest from release to report. No reduction permitted.
3) If over 14:00: confirm the duty period is authorized by 121.467(b)(4)-(6) with a qualifying mid-duty rest opportunity, then confirm 12:00 rest, or a reduced 10:00 rest paired with a 14:00 makeup rest beginning within 24 hours of the reduced rest's start.
4) Confirm the rest block is free of all restraint, standby, and duty responsibility.
5) Confirm 24 consecutive hours free from all duty within each 7 consecutive calendar days.
6) Confirm any CBA or manual provision meets or exceeds these figures; if the CBA states a higher scheduled floor (e.g., 10:00 scheduled plus an 8:00 behind-the-door actual minimum), the higher/contractual provision controls the carrier's obligation.

BOTTOM LINE: 10 consecutive hours between duty periods for a Part 121 flight attendant, non-reducible, measured release-to-report; 12 hours (reducible only to 10, with a 14-hour makeup rest within 24 hours) after an extended duty period of more than 14 hours.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-121/subpart-p/subject-group-ecfrb49759e744c709b/section-121.467 and 9 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.1062. The first reads: "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."

question: H3
answer:
ANSWER

A drone counts as a 'small unmanned aircraft' (small drone / sUAS) under FAA rules only if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS on takeoff — including everything on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft. 55 lb is a ceiling you must stay under, not a weight you may reach. Exactly 55.0 lb is not a small drone.

- Limit: < 55 lb (strict)
- Metric equivalent: 55 lb = 24.9476 kg, so the metric statement of the limit is < 24.95 kg. A drone at exactly 25 kg (55.116 lb) is NOT a small drone, even though FAA summary materials casually render '55 lbs. (25 kg)'. Build to 24.9 kg / 54.9 lb or below to leave margin.
- Grams: 55 lb = 24,947.6 g.

CONTROLLING RULE

14 CFR 107.3 (Definitions), current text:
  'Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'

14 CFR 107.1 / Part 107 scope, and FAA AIM 11-1-1: 'Part 107 operations are limited to small UAS (sUAS) weighing less than 55 pounds.' FAA's Part 107 summary: 'Unmanned aircraft must weigh less than 55 lbs. (25 kg).'

WHAT IS COUNTED IN THE 55 POUNDS

The weight is the aircraft's takeoff weight with everything aboard or attached:
- airframe, motors, propellers, ESCs, flight controller
- battery or fuel, full at takeoff
- cameras, gimbals, sensors, antennas, parachutes, lights
- any payload or cargo, and external loads (securely attached objects count)
The ground-side equipment — control station, tablet, controller, batteries for the controller, visual observer's gear — is part of the UAS but is NOT part of the aircraft and is not counted against the 55 lb aircraft limit.

WHAT HAPPENS AT AND ABOVE 55 POUNDS

- Part 107 no longer applies. The 55 lb figure lives in the definition of 'small unmanned aircraft,' and the Part 107 waiver provision (107.205) does not list that definition — there is no Part 107 waiver that authorizes operating a 55 lb-or-heavier aircraft as a small UAS.
- The aircraft becomes a 'large UAS' (FAA AIM: 'Large UAS (MGOW 55 Pounds or More)'). Non-recreational civil operations move to 14 CFR Part 91 UAS operations: experimental airworthiness certificate under 14 CFR 21.191, compliance with applicable Part 91 rules, and an FAA Certificate of Authorization (COA) or other airspace authorization. Public aircraft operations follow the public-aircraft pathway (AC 00-1.1).
- Registration shifts from the Part 48 online system to 14 CFR Part 47 aircraft registration.

COMMERCIAL VS. RECREATIONAL — DOES THE NUMBER CHANGE?

No. The FAA frames both pathways on small UAS under 55 lb:
- Non-recreational/commercial: 14 CFR Part 107, default rule for drones under 55 lb. Every Part 107 UAS must be registered regardless of weight.
- Recreational: the Exception for Limited Recreational Operations (49 U.S.C. 44809). The FAA applies the same small-UAS framing; a drone of 55 lb or more is outside both the Part 107 rule and the recreational exception. Registration is required above 0.55 lb.
So the answer to 'how heavy can a drone be and still count as a small drone' is the same 55 lb line either way. What changes with use is the operating rules, not the weight ceiling.

DO NOT CONFUSE THESE LOWER THRESHOLDS WITH THE 'SMALL DRONE' LINE

- 0.55 lb (249.5 g ≈ 250 g) — Part 107 Category 1 operations (14 CFR 107.110(a)(1)): aircraft must weigh 0.55 lb or less on takeoff and throughout the operation, and have no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate skin. This is a sub-category of small UAS, not the definition of one.
- 0.55 lb (250 g) — recreational flyers must register a UAS above this weight; at or below it, registration is not required for recreational flight. (Part 107 operations must register at any weight.)
- Category 2 and Category 3 (14 CFR 107.115, 107.125) are about operations over people and require an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance; they do not raise the 55 lb ceiling.

QUICK REFERENCE

| Threshold | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Small UAS ceiling | < 55 lb (< 24.95 kg) | Eligible for Part 107 / recreational exception |
| Large UAS | >= 55 lb (>= 24.95 kg) | Out of Part 107; Part 91 + experimental certificate + COA |
| Category 1 / recreational registration | <= 0.55 lb (<= 249.5 g) | Category 1 ops; no recreational registration required |
| Registration (recreational) | > 0.55 lb (> 250 g) | Must register via FAA DroneZone (Part 48) |

PLAIN-LANGUAGE VERSION FOR THE REQUESTER

'Under FAA rules a drone is a small drone if it weighs less than 55 pounds at takeoff, with battery, camera, payload and anything attached included. That is about 24.95 kg, so keep the all-up weight under about 24.9 kg to be safe. At 55 pounds or more it is no longer a small drone: Part 107 does not apply, and you would need the Part 91 / experimental certificate / COA route. Separately, if it weighs 0.55 lb (250 g) or less you also get the lightest treatment — that is the Category 1 line and the recreational registration line — but the answer to "how heavy can a small drone be" is 55 pounds.'

CAVEATS

- This is U.S. federal FAA regulation. Other authorities (EASA, Transport Canada, CAA) use different limits (e.g., EASA open category 25 kg / 900 g sub-limits).
- State/local ordinances and insurance policies can impose lower weight-based requirements but cannot raise the federal ceiling.
- The 55 lb figure is current as of the eCFR text of 14 CFR 107.3 (amended by Amdt. 107-8, 86 FR 4381, Jan. 15, 2021) and FAA AIM Chapter 11.

question: H5
answer:
BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL (FAA, 14 CFR 91.155(a), Table; AIM 3-1-4 / TBL 3-1-1)

1. THE ANSWER

Class E airspace, less than 10,000 ft MSL:
  - Flight visibility: 3 statute miles
  - Distance from clouds: 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal

That is the complete requirement. It is the same figure by day and by night — the Class E row below 10,000 ft MSL contains no day/night split (unlike the Class G rows). There is no 'clear of clouds' option in Class E; 'clear of clouds' applies to Class B and to Class G at 1,200 ft AGL or less by day.

Regulatory text (14 CFR 91.155(a)): 'Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section and Sec. 91.157, no person may operate an aircraft under VFR when the flight visibility is less, or at a distance from clouds that is less, than that prescribed for the corresponding altitude and class of airspace in the following table.' The Class E entry reads: 'Less than 10,000 feet MSL — 3 statute miles — 500 feet below; 1,000 feet above; 2,000 feet horizontal.' AIM TBL 3-1-1 reproduces the identical values.

2. WHAT 'BELOW 10,000 FT MSL' DOES AND DOES NOT KEY TO

- The Class E row is keyed to MSL altitude only, not to height above ground. Class E at 700 ft AGL, at 1,200 ft AGL, and at 5,000 ft AGL all use the same 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 figures, so long as the aircraft is below 10,000 ft MSL.
- Class E surface areas (the dashed-magenta areas designated to the surface for an airport) use this same 'less than 10,000 ft MSL' row for visibility and cloud clearance. Surface-area status adds two separate constraints, below.
- 14 CFR 91.155(e): 'an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E airspace area is considered to be within the airspace directly below that area.' An aircraft exactly at the floor of a Class E shelf is therefore governed by the Class E minimums, not by the Class G minimums beneath the shelf.
- Per AIM 3-1-3, where designations overlap, the more restrictive applies; Class E is more restrictive than Class G. So an aircraft in Class E may not fall back on the more permissive Class G day figures (1 SM, clear of clouds).

3. ADJACENT ROWS — STATED SO THEY ARE NOT CONFUSED WITH THE ANSWER

Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL (NOT applicable below 10,000):
  5 statute miles; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 statute mile horizontal.

Class G, 1,200 ft or less above the surface (for comparison only):
  Airplane, day: 1 SM, clear of clouds. Airplane, night: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. Helicopter, day: 1/2 SM, clear of clouds. Helicopter, night: 1 SM, clear of clouds.

Class G, more than 1,200 ft above the surface but less than 10,000 ft MSL:
  Day: 1 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. Night: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal.

Class B: 3 SM, clear of clouds. Class C and Class D: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. Class A: not applicable (VFR not authorized).

Note the structural point a pilot must not miss: in Class G the visibility and cloud clearance change with day/night and with height above the surface; in Class E below 10,000 ft MSL neither of those variables changes anything. Only crossing 10,000 ft MSL changes the Class E figures.

4. ADDITIONAL CONSTRAINTS THAT APPLY WITHIN A CLASS E SURFACE AREA (91.155(c) and (d))

These are separate from the visibility/cloud-clearance table and are frequently conflated with it:
- 91.155(c): except under 91.157 (special VFR), no VFR flight beneath the ceiling within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport when the ceiling is less than 1,000 ft.
- 91.155(d): no takeoff, landing, or entry into the traffic pattern under VFR within the surface areas of Class B, C, D, or E airspace designated for an airport unless ground visibility is at least 3 statute miles, or — if ground visibility is not reported — flight visibility during takeoff, landing, or in the traffic pattern is at least 3 statute miles.
So at a Class E surface-area airport the practical floor is: ceiling at least 1,000 ft, visibility at least 3 SM (ground or flight, as applicable), plus the standard 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 once airborne.

5. EXCLUSIONS FROM THE BASIC FIGURES (not applied here, listed for completeness)

- Special VFR (91.157): ATC clearance, clear of clouds, at least 1 SM flight visibility (except helicopters), and — for other than helicopters — between sunrise and sunset unless the pilot is instrument-qualified and the aircraft is equipped per 91.205(d).
- 91.155(b)(1): helicopter clear of clouds in an airport traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway or helipad, flight visibility not less than 1/2 SM.
- 91.155(b)(2): airplane, powered parachute, or weight-shift-control aircraft clear of clouds in an airport traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway at night with visibility at least 1 SM but less than 3 SM.
These are special provisions, not the 'basic VFR' answer requested.

6. UNIT CONVERSIONS (approximate, for readers working in metric)

3 statute miles = 4.83 km (about 4.8 km). 500 ft = 152 m. 1,000 ft = 305 m. 2,000 ft = 610 m. The regulation is written in statute miles and feet; the metric values are informational only.

7. BASIS, SCOPE AND CAVEATS

- Source: 14 CFR 91.155(a) table (eCFR, current; GovInfo CFR-2025-title14-vol2) and FAA AIM 3-1-4 / TBL 3-1-1. Both sources agree exactly.
- Jurisdiction: this answer is FAA (United States). The request's use of 'Class E' and 'MSL' matches the FAA frame. Other jurisdictions publish different tables in metric units (ICAO Annex 2 / EASA SERA use a 5 km visibility and 1,500 m horizontal / 1,000 ft vertical clearance below 10,000 ft for Class E). Those figures are outside the fetched sources and are flagged here only so the answer is not misapplied outside U.S. airspace; verify against the governing national AIP before use.
- These are legal minimums, not safe margins. Collision-avoidance responsibility under see-and-avoid (14 CFR 91.113) is unaffected; 91.155 confers no traffic separation. Marginal VFR at exactly 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 leaves essentially no room for error, and the minimums assume the pilot can actually see and avoid traffic and terrain.
- 'Basic VFR' here means the 91.155(a) table figures, exclusive of special VFR, the 91.155(b) traffic-pattern provisions, and any waivers or letters of agreement.

question: H7
answer:
OSHA PERMISSIBLE EXPOSURE LIMIT AND ACTION LEVEL FOR RESPIRABLE CRYSTALLINE SILICA — GENERAL INDUSTRY

SCOPE AND BASIS OF THE ANSWER
Jurisdiction: U.S. federal OSHA, general industry. Governing provision: 29 CFR 1910.1053, "Respirable crystalline silica" (the 2016 final rule, 81 Fed. Reg. 16286, effective June 23, 2016; all obligations commenced June 23, 2018 except the limited oil-and-gas hydraulic-fracturing and medical-surveillance phase-ins in paragraph (l)). This is not the construction standard (29 CFR 1926.1153) and not the maritime/shipyard provisions.

1. THE TWO VALUES

| Parameter | Value | Averaging basis | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permissible exposure limit (PEL) | 50 µg/m³ (0.050 mg/m³) | 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) | 29 CFR 1910.1053(c) |
| Action level (AL) | 25 µg/m³ (0.025 mg/m³) | 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) | 29 CFR 1910.1053(b), definition of "Action level" |

Verbatim regulatory text:
- (c) Permissible exposure limit (PEL). "The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."
- (b) Definitions. "Action level means a concentration of airborne respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

Direct answer as a safety engineer would state it to an operations audience: the federal general-industry PEL for respirable crystalline silica is 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air as an 8-hour TWA; the action level is 25 µg/m³ as an 8-hour TWA, i.e., one-half the PEL.

2. WHAT THE NUMBERS COVER (important, and a common source of error)
- "Respirable crystalline silica" is defined in 1910.1053(b) as "quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite contained in airborne particles that are determined to be respirable by a sampling device designed to meet the characteristics for respirable-particle-size-selective samplers specified in ISO 7708:1995." There is ONE limit covering all three polymorphs collectively — the standard does not set separate quartz, cristobalite and tridymite limits, and cristobalite/tridymite are not given a lower multiplier as they were under some older consensus criteria.
- The limit applies to the respirable particle-size fraction only (ISO 7708:1995 convention, conventionally approximated by a 4 mm nylon cyclone at 2.5 L/min or an equivalent ISO/CEN selector). Total dust sampling does not demonstrate compliance with this PEL.
- The limit is a mass-based concentration with no percent-silica divisor. Unlike the older Table Z-1 formula limit, the 50 µg/m³ PEL applies regardless of the quartz content of the bulk material. A material that is only a few percent crystalline silica still must meet 50 µg/m³ respirable crystalline silica.
- "Employee exposure" is defined as the exposure that would occur if the employee were not using a respirator. Respirators are not a means of achieving compliance; they are supplementary (paragraph (f)) and are only credited in the manner the standard allows.
- There is no ceiling or short-term exposure limit in 1910.1053. The PEL is an 8-hour TWA only. (Do not carry over a peak/ceiling concept from other substance standards.)

3. WHY THE ACTION LEVEL MATTERS (the practical consequence of the 25 µg/m³ figure)
The action level is not merely an alarm; it is the trigger for the standard's assessment and medical-surveillance machinery:
- 1910.1053(d)(1): the employer must assess the exposure of each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level (25 µg/m³, 8-hr TWA), using either the performance option (d)(2) or the scheduled monitoring option (d)(3).
- Medical surveillance under (i)(1) is triggered for employees exposed at or above the action level for 30 or more days per year, and separately for employees exposed above the PEL for 30 or more days per year (see also the phase-in dates in (l)(4): June 23, 2018 for the above-PEL/30-day group; June 23, 2020 for the at-or-above-AL/30-day group).
- "Regulated area" (b) is any area demarcated by the employer where exposure exceeds, or can reasonably be expected to exceed, the PEL (50 µg/m³).
- Engineering and work practice controls are required where feasible, and where they cannot get exposures to or below the PEL the employer must still use them to reduce exposure to the lowest feasible level and supplement with respiratory protection (paragraph (f)).

4. COMPARING A SAMPLE RESULT TO THE LIMITS — WORKED EXAMPLES
Rule: convert the laboratory result to an 8-hour TWA before comparing to 25 or 50 µg/m³.
TWA(8-hr) = (C_sample x T_sample) / 8, with C in µg/m³ and T in hours (assuming zero exposure for the unsampled remainder; adjust if there are other measured segments).

| Case | Sample result | 8-hr TWA | Comparison |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 70 µg/m³ for 6.5 h | 70 x 6.5 / 8 = 56.9 µg/m³ | Above PEL (50) — overexposure; controls + respiratory protection required |
| B | 62 µg/m³ for 8 h | 62.0 µg/m³ | Above PEL (50) |
| C | 48 µg/m³ for 8 h (0.048 mg/m³) | 48.0 µg/m³ | Below PEL, at/above AL (25) — exposure assessment and surveillance obligations triggered |
| D | 31 µg/m³ for 8 h | 31.0 µg/m³ | Below PEL, above AL |
| E | 18 µg/m³ for 8 h | 18.0 µg/m³ | Below AL — no (d)(1) assessment obligation on this result alone |

Note that in Case A the sample concentration (70) is not itself the compliance metric; the 56.9 µg/m³ 8-hour TWA is, and it still exceeds 50. Conversely, a short high sample can fall below the PEL once averaged — but see the exposure-assessment and controls obligations, which do not disappear merely because a single TWA lands under 50.

5. SAMPLING AND ANALYSIS (so the number is defensible)
- Collect the respirable fraction with an ISO 7708:1995-conforming size-selective sampler (e.g., 4 mm cyclone at 2.5 L/min, or a GK2.69/ISO selector) on an appropriate filter, per 1910.1053 Appendix A and the OSHA Technical Manual (TED 01-00-015) sampling chapter.
- Analysis is by X-ray diffraction (NIOSH 7500 is the method most commonly used for quartz/cristobalite/tridymite) or by IR (NIOSH 7602/7603) or OSHA ID-142, as listed in Appendix A to §1910.1053. Confirm the exact method list against the current Appendix A text before writing the sampling plan; the method must be capable of quantifying each polymorph present and of meeting the required limit of detection at the action level.
- Report results as µg/m³ respirable crystalline silica, 8-hour TWA, with the sampling duration, flow rate, and analytical method stated. LOD/LOQ must be low enough to distinguish below-AL from at/above-AL (practically, LOQ well under 25 µg/m³ for an 8-hour sample).

6. HISTORICAL / SUPERSEDED LIMITS (do not use for compliance)
Before the 2016 rule, general industry respirable crystalline silica was governed by the formula limit in 29 CFR 1910.1000 Table Z-1: respirable quartz = 10 mg/m³ ÷ (%SiO2 + 2); total dust quartz = 30 mg/m³ ÷ (%SiO2 + 2). That formula is content-dependent (for 100% quartz it computes to about 0.098 mg/m³, i.e., ~98 µg/m³; for 10% quartz it computes to about 0.83 mg/m³). It is not the operative limit for general industry today: 1910.1053 sets a single 50 µg/m³ PEL and 25 µg/m³ AL independent of percent silica, and OSHA enforces against 1910.1053. Any program document still citing the Z-1 formula for general industry should be revised.

7. JURISDICTION CAVEAT (state-plan states)
About half the states and two territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans, which must be at least as effective as federal OSHA but may adopt different or more stringent limits. Example: California's Table AC-7 lists respirable crystalline silica at 0.025 mg/m³ (25 µg/m³) as an 8-hour TWA, which is stricter than the federal PEL. Before finalizing any exposure limit in a written program, confirm the applicable State Plan's silica rule and effective date. The 50/25 µg/m³ figures above are the federal OSHA figures.

8. BOUNDARY WITH CONSTRUCTION AND MARITIME
- Construction: 29 CFR 1926.1153, which uses the same 50 µg/m³ PEL and 25 µg/m³ AL but adds the Table 1 task-based compliance option.
- 1910.1053(a)(3) provides a narrow carve-out: the general-industry section does not apply if the employer complies with 1926.1153 and (i) the task performed is indistinguishable from a construction task listed on Table 1 of 1926.1153, and (ii) the task will not be performed regularly in the same environment and conditions.
- Maritime/shipyard work is covered by 29 CFR 1915 (with 1915.1000 Table Z for air contaminants), not by 1910.1053. Do not apply the general-industry figures to shipyard employment without checking Part 1915.

9. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A PROGRAM DOCUMENT
"Federal OSHA general industry (29 CFR 1910.1053): PEL = 50 µg/m³ respirable crystalline silica, 8-hour TWA; Action Level = 25 µg/m³, 8-hour TWA. Both apply to quartz, cristobalite and tridymite collectively, in the ISO 7708:1995 respirable fraction, measured as the exposure that would occur without a respirator."

SOURCES
- 29 CFR 1910.1053 (eCFR, current) — paragraphs (b), (c), (d)(1), (f), (l), and Appendix A.
- 29 CFR 1910.1053 as published in the 2016, 2023 and 2024 editions of Title 29 CFR (identical PEL and AL text in each).
- 81 Fed. Reg. 16286 (Mar. 25, 2016) — final rule.

question: H11
answer:
Answer: the 1876 first edition of Robert's Rules of Order requires a two-thirds vote to adopt a motion for the Previous Question.

Scope and reading of the ask:
- Source edition: the 1876 first edition, the pocket manual carried by Project Gutenberg (etext 9097 is the relevant Gutenberg text for that manual).
- 'Adopt a motion for the Previous Question' is read as the vote needed to order/carry the Previous Question itself — i.e., to close debate and bring the pending question to an immediate vote — not the vote later taken on the underlying pending question.

Rule and location:
- In the 1876 edition the motion is treated in the article headed 'Previous Question' (Article VI in the 1876 arrangement) and in the manual's table/list of motions.
- The manual's rule is that the Previous Question requires a two-thirds vote. In the 1876 scheme the Previous Question is a non-debatable motion to bring the assembly to a vote on the pending question; it is adopted only by a two-thirds vote.

Application:
- If the affirmative vote on ordering the Previous Question is less than two-thirds, the motion is not adopted and debate continues.
- If the affirmative vote is two-thirds or more, the Previous Question is adopted and the pending question is put.
- The two-thirds requirement is the adoption threshold for the Previous Question. The separate vote on the underlying question is governed by that question's own threshold; the Previous Question motion does not itself change it.

Citation verification note:
- The supplied Gutenberg page-fetch cache returned no quotable passage, so the exact transcription sentence should be verified against Gutenberg etext 9097 before publication. The section to cite is the article headed 'Previous Question'; the operative rule is the manual's two-thirds vote requirement.

question: H13
answer:
# Luminous efficacy Kcd in the SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019)

## 1. Direct answer

| Quantity | Fixed value | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation, Kcd (ask 1) | **683** (exact, no uncertainty) | **lm W⁻¹** (= lm/W = cd sr W⁻¹ = cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³) |
| Frequency of that monochromatic radiation (ask 2) | **540 × 10¹² Hz** (= 540 THz) | **Hz** |

Both numbers come from the definition of the SI base unit of luminous intensity, the candela, and from the table of the seven defining constants of the revised SI. The value 683 lm/W is a *defining* value: it is exact by definition (no measurement uncertainty, infinite significant figures), fixed since 20 May 2019 by the 26th CGPM.

## 2. Verbatim source text (full Brochure, §2.3.1 "The candela")

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹, which is equal to cd sr W⁻¹, or cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ∆νCs."

> "This definition implies the exact relation Kcd = 683 cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 × 10¹² Hz. Inverting this relation gives an exact expression for the candela in terms of the defining constants Kcd, h and ∆νCs:
> 1 cd = (Kcd/683) kg m² s⁻³ sr⁻¹
> which is equal to
> 1 cd = [1/683] (6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴)(9 192 631 770)² (∆νCs)² h Kcd ≈ 2.614 8305 × 10¹⁰ (∆νCs)² h Kcd."

> "The effect of this definition is that one candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W sr⁻¹."

## 3. Verbatim source text (defining-constants list, revised SI)

> "• the Avogadro constant, NA, is 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ mol⁻¹,
> • the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, Kcd, is 683 lm/W,
> where the hertz, joule, coulomb, lumen, and watt, with unit symbols Hz, J, C, lm, and W, respectively, are related to the units second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela … according to Hz = s⁻¹, J = kg m² s⁻², C = A s, lm = cd sr, and W = kg m² s⁻³."

So in the Brochure's own defining-constants table (Table 4 of the 9th edition) the entry reads: **Kcd = 683 lm W⁻¹**, with the frequency stated inline: **540 × 10¹² Hz**.

## 4. Corroborating restatement (CCPR mise en pratique, Appendix 2 to the 9th edition)

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹, which is equal to cd sr W⁻¹, or cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ …"

and, for the wavelength equivalent (useful cross-check, not part of the asks):

> "f_a = 555.017 nm is the wavelength in standard air at the frequency of 540 × 10¹² Hz given in the definition of Kcd …"

## 5. What the two answers mean, and what they do not mean

- **683 is not a measured efficiency.** It is the exactly fixed numerical value of a defining constant. Any realization of the candela, lumen, lux or cd m⁻² must be consistent with it; the associated *measurement* uncertainty belongs to the realization, not to Kcd.
- **The frequency is fixed; the wavelength is not part of the definition.** ν = 540 × 10¹² Hz (540 THz) corresponds to λ ≈ 555.17 nm in vacuum and to λ = 555.017 nm in standard air (the mise en pratique value). These two wavelengths differ only because of the refractive index of air; the definition is stated in frequency precisely to avoid that ambiguity.
- **Other frequencies.** The definition fixes Kcd at one frequency only. For radiation at other frequencies, photometric quantities are obtained by weighting the spectral power distribution with the CIE spectral luminous efficiency function V(λ) and converting to absolute values with the same Kcd (mise en pratique §3.1).
- **Historical continuity.** The same pair (683 lm/W at 540 × 10¹² Hz) was adopted by the CIPM in 1977 and used in the 1979 (16th CGPM) definition of the candela, which defined the candela as the luminous intensity of a source emitting monochromatic radiation at 540 × 10¹² Hz with a radiant intensity of 1/683 W sr⁻¹. The 2019 revision did not change the number; it changed its *status* — from a defined property of an idealized source to the fixed numerical value of a defining constant, thereby defining the unit via the exact relation Kcd = 683 cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³. Earlier, pre-1979 photometric units (e.g. the 1946 "new candle") were not tied to this exact value, so care is needed when citing "683 lm/W" against pre-1979 editions: the number is a post-1977/1979 SI value.

## 6. Notation conventions used above (per the Brochure's own style rules)

- Groups of three digits are separated by a thin space, never by a comma or a point: "683", "6.022 140 76 × 10²³", "2.614 8305 × 10¹⁰".
- The multiplication sign is ×, with a space on each side; powers of ten are written 10¹², 10⁻³⁴, etc.
- Unit symbols are upright and separated from the numerical value by a space: "683 lm W⁻¹", "540 × 10¹² Hz".
- "lm W⁻¹" may be written "lm/W" without change of meaning; the Brochure uses both forms.

## 7. Sources consulted

1. BIPM, *The International System of Units (SI Brochure)*, 9th edition (2019), §2.3.1 "The candela" and Table 4 (defining constants) — https://www.bipm.org/documents/20126/41483022/SI-Brochure-9-EN.pdf/2d2b50bf-f2b4-9661-f402-5f9d66e4b507?version=4.0 (accessed 2026-11-17).
2. BIPM, *SI Brochure*, 9th edition — concise summary (version 4.01), defining-constants list — https://www.bipm.org/documents/20126/41483022/SI-Brochure-9-concise-EN.pdf/2fda4656-e236-0fcb-3867-36ca74eea4e3 (accessed 2026-11-17).
3. CIPM/CCPR, *Mise en pratique for the definition of the candela and associated derived units … in the SI*, SI Brochure 9th edition, Appendix 2, v1.02, 22 March 2021, §2 and §3.1 — https://www.bipm.org/documents/20126/41489685/SI-App2-candela.pdf/1603b2e8-64a3-1fda-d9b4-7b748bad9c01 (accessed 2026-11-17).
4. NIST, *SI Units – Luminous Intensity* (secondary corroboration of the identical wording) — https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/si-units-luminous-intensity (accessed 2026-11-17).

Caveat on citation granularity: the section numbers (§2.3.1, Table 4, Appendix 2 §2) are those of the 9th edition as published online; the printed-edition page numbers were not verified and should be confirmed against a physical or paginated PDF copy if a page-level citation is required. Translations of the Brochure render the wording differently (e.g. "683 lumen per watt", "540 × 10¹² hertz") but do not alter either number.

answer:
# Regulatory determination — flash point 65 °C, no other hazard class (US HMR, 49 CFR)

## 1. Bottom line

**No. A liquid with a flash point of 65 °C (149 °F) is not a Class 3 flammable liquid.** The Class 3 flash-point ceiling in 49 CFR 173.120(a) is *not more than 60 °C (140 °F)*; 65 °C exceeds it by 5 °C (9 °F).

Because the material has a flash point **above 60 °C and below 93 °C** and (as stated) meets the definition of no other hazard class, it is a **combustible liquid** under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1). “Combustible liquid” is a US-domestic regulatory category, not a hazard class — it carries no class number and is not a Class 3 material.

Practical consequence: in **non-bulk** packagings it is excepted from the HMR entirely unless it is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant (§173.150(f)(2)); in **bulk** packagings, or if it is a hazardous substance/waste/marine pollutant, only a limited list of requirements continues to apply (§173.150(f)(3), beginning with shipping papers, package marking, and identification numbers on bulk packages).

The “No” is conditional on two facts that were not supplied; both are stated in §5 below (intentional heating in bulk; sustain-combustion test).

## 2. Governing text and edition relied on

| Provision | Operative text |
|---|---|
| 49 CFR 173.120(a) | “a **flammable liquid** (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging…” |
| 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1) | “a **combustible liquid** means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F).” |
| 49 CFR 173.120(b)(3) | “A combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion is not subject to the requirements of this subchapter as a combustible liquid.” (ASTM D 4206 or appendix H procedure) |
| 49 CFR 173.150(f)(2) | HMR do not apply to a combustible liquid in a **non-bulk** packaging unless it is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant. |
| 49 CFR 173.150(f)(3) | A combustible liquid in a **bulk** packaging (or one that is a hazardous substance/waste/marine pollutant) is not subject to the subchapter except those requirements pertaining to (i) shipping papers/waybills/switching orders/manifests, (ii) marking of packages, (iii) display of identification numbers on bulk packages, and the items that follow in that paragraph. |

**Edition control:** the 60 °C / 93 °C thresholds are identical in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions of 49 CFR (Parts 171–180) reviewed for this determination, so the answer is stable across those editions. Earlier editions were not verified in this record and are not relied on. (Historically the HMR used a 100 °F / 37.8 °C flammable ceiling; that is not the text in force and is not used here.)

## 3. Numeric tests applied

| Test | Threshold in the rule | Subject liquid | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Class 3 flash-point ceiling, §173.120(a) | FP ≤ 60 °C (140 °F) | 65 °C (149 °F) | **Fails by 5 °C → not Class 3** |
| Elevated-temperature limb, §173.120(a) | FP ≥ 37.8 °C (100 °F) **and** intentionally heated **and** offered/transported at or above FP **and** bulk packaging | 65 ≥ 37.8 (first element met); heating/bulk status not established | Not triggered on the facts given |
| Combustible liquid band, §173.120(b)(1) | 60 °C < FP < 93 °C (200 °F) | 60 < 65 < 93 | **Met → combustible liquid** |
| “No other hazard class,” §173.120(b)(1) | Must not meet another class definition | Taken as given | Met |
| Sustain-combustion disqualifier, §173.120(b)(3) | If it does not sustain combustion → not regulated as a combustible liquid | Not tested | Open (see §5, K2) |
| 93 °C mixture exemption, §173.150(f)(4) | FP ≥ 93 °C | 65 °C | Not applicable |

Unit conversions used, checked against the regulation's own parentheticals: 37.8 °C = 100 °F; 60 °C = 140 °F; 65 °C = 149 °F; 93 °C = 199.4 °F, printed as 200 °F.

## 4. Classification logic, step by step

1. **Confirm the physical state.** The definition applies to liquids. The material is stated to be a liquid; note that a material that is not a liquid at 37.8 °C (100 °F) is outside the Class 3 liquid definition and this analysis would not apply.
2. **Apply the Class 3 flash-point ceiling.** §173.120(a) sets the ceiling at *not more than 60 °C*. 65 °C is greater than 60 °C. The first limb of the Class 3 definition therefore fails.
3. **Check the elevated-temperature limb.** The second limb of §173.120(a) captures liquids with FP ≥ 37.8 °C that are intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above their flash point in a bulk packaging. The flash-point element is satisfied (65 ≥ 37.8), but heating, actual transport temperature and bulk status are unstated. On the facts given (ambient, unheated), this limb is not triggered. **If it is triggered, the material is Class 3 and the answer flips — see K1.**
4. **Check the §173.120(a)(1)–(5) exceptions.** These exclude certain liquids from Class 3 (Class 9 liquids per §173.115; mixtures ≥99% of components with FP ≥60 °C not transported at/above their flash point; FP > 35 °C liquids that do not sustain combustion; FP > 35 °C with fire point > 100 °C per ISO 2592; FP > 35 °C water-miscible solutions with > 90% water). They are moot for the class question here because the material already fails the 60 °C ceiling and cannot be Class 3 in the first place — they matter only to the parallel question of whether a material *below* 60 °C escapes Class 3. The sustain-combustion concept reappears at §173.120(b)(3) and is addressed in K2.
5. **Apply the combustible-liquid definition.** §173.120(b)(1) requires (i) not meeting any other hazard class — given — and (ii) a flash point above 60 °C and below 93 °C — 65 °C satisfies both bounds. The material is a combustible liquid.
6. **Do not reclass.** §173.120(b)(2)/§173.150(f)(1) permits a *flammable* liquid with FP ≥ 38 °C to be **reclassed** as a combustible liquid. That mechanism is not used here and is not needed: the material is a combustible liquid by direct application of §173.120(b)(1), because it was never a flammable liquid. (The reclassing route would also be unavailable for vessel or aircraft transport except where other means of transport is impracticable.)
7. **Determine the regulatory consequence.** Apply §173.150(f)(2)/(3) against the packaging type and the hazardous-substance / hazardous-waste / marine-pollutant status (see §6).
8. **Do not assign a class, UN number or packing group as a Class 3 material.** No Class 3 packing group is assigned because the material is not Class 3. If it later becomes Class 3 through the elevated-temperature limb, packing group is assigned under §173.121 — with a flash point of 65 °C and any initial boiling point above 35 °C, that would land in PG III.

## 5. What would change the answer (kill conditions for this determination)

- **K1 — Intentional heating in bulk.** If the liquid is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above 65 °C in a **bulk** packaging, the second limb of §173.120(a) makes it a **Class 3 flammable liquid** notwithstanding the 65 °C flash point. §173.120(b)(2) expressly bars reclassing such an elevated-temperature material as a combustible liquid. This is the single most important condition on the “No.”
- **K2 — Does not sustain combustion.** If the material fails to sustain combustion when tested by ASTM D 4206 or the appendix H procedure, §173.120(b)(3) removes it from regulation *as a combustible liquid* — i.e., it becomes unregulated rather than a combustible liquid. No test data was supplied; this is open.
- **K3 — Another hazard class applies.** §173.120(b)(1) requires that the liquid “does not meet the definition of any other hazard class.” That is accepted as given here. If re-screening showed, for example, a Class 9 (miscellaneous) or Class 8 (corrosive) or Class 6.1 (toxic) definition was met, the material would be classified in that class and would not be a combustible liquid at all.
- **K4 — Flash point re-determined at ≤ 60 °C.** If a conforming closed-cup re-test returns ≤ 60 °C, the material is Class 3 by the first limb of §173.120(a).
- **K5 — Non-US or international mode.** IMDG / ICAO / IATA / ADR are outside the scope assumed here. Note for the record: those regimes also use a 60 °C ceiling, so a 65 °C liquid is not Class 3 there either, but they have **no “combustible liquid” category** — the material would generally be unregulated except for elevated-temperature-substance provisions (e.g. UN3257), marine-pollutant/environmentally-hazardous-substance provisions, or domestic modal variations. Those must be evaluated separately if the shipment goes by vessel or aircraft.

## 6. Record gaps and data needed to close the file

1. **Flash-point method.** §173.120(c) prescribes closed-cup procedures: ASTM D 56, D 3278 or D 3828 for a homogeneous single-phase liquid with viscosity < 45 S.U.S. at 38 °C that does not form a surface film; ASTM D 93 (Pensky-Martens) for other liquids. An open-cup value is not acceptable. The 65 °C figure is assumed to come from a conforming closed-cup test with no correction required. Because the margin to the 60 °C threshold is only 5 °C and closed-cup repeatability is on the order of a couple of degrees, the margin is adequate but not generous — a conforming re-test should be on file.
2. **Packaging type (bulk vs non-bulk)** and **hazardous substance (RQ) / hazardous waste / marine pollutant status.** These decide whether §173.150(f)(2) (no HMR) or §173.150(f)(3) (limited requirements) applies. A combustible liquid that is also a hazardous substance, hazardous waste or marine pollutant is regulated even in non-bulk packagings.
3. **Heating and transport temperature** (feeds K1), and **bulk status** (feeds both K1 and §173.150(f)).
4. **Sustain-combustion data** (feeds K2).
5. **Shipping description, if one is required** (bulk, or hazardous substance/waste/marine pollutant). For domestic shipments the Hazardous Materials Table provides a domestic “Combustible liquid, n.o.s.” entry under NA1993; confirm the class column, label column and packing group for that entry in the current §172.101 Table before it is used on a shipping paper. It is not asserted here because it was not verified in this record.
6. **Independent regimes.** “Not regulated as Class 3 under the HMR” does not mean non-hazardous: OSHA Hazard Communication / GHS classification (which uses a 60 °C / 93 °C scheme with categories 3 and 4), RCRA waste determination, and state fire code (flammable/combustible liquid storage) all apply independently of DOT transport status.

## 7. Audit trail — citations relied on

- 49 CFR 173.120(a), (b)(1)–(3), (c) — Class 3 definitions, combustible liquid definition, sustain-combustion rule, flash-point test methods. (49 CFR 173.120, 2025 edition, govinfo; identical text in the eCFR current version.)
- 49 CFR 173.150(f)(1)–(4) — combustible liquid exceptions: reclassing (not used here), non-bulk exception, bulk/HS/HW/MP limited requirements, ≥93 °C mixture exemption. (49 CFR 173.150, 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions — thresholds identical.)
- 49 CFR 173.121 — packing group assignment for Class 3 (relevant only under K1).
- 49 CFR 172.101 — Hazardous Materials Table (relevant only if a shipping description is required; to be verified before use).

question: H17
answer:
NRC PUBLIC DOSE LIMITS — 10 CFR PART 20, SUBPART D

SOURCES: eCFR, 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D, §§ 20.1301 and 20.1302 (current as of the 2026-11-17 fetch; source note '56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 48625, Sept. 20, 1995; 62 FR 4133, Jan. 29, 1997; 67 FR 20370, Apr. 24, 2002; 67 FR 62872, Oct. 9, 2002').

=====================================================================
1. THE TWO LIMITS (HEADLINE ANSWER)
=====================================================================

(A) ANNUAL LIMIT — 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1)
    Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) to individual members of the public
    from the licensed operation: 0.1 rem in a year = 100 mrem/yr = 1 mSv/yr.
    Basis: all pathways, external + internal (inhalation, ingestion, immersion).

(B) ANY-ONE-HOUR LIMIT IN AN UNRESTRICTED AREA — 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2)
    Dose in any unrestricted area from EXTERNAL SOURCES: 0.002 rem in any one
    hour = 2 mrem/h = 0.02 mSv/h = 20 uSv/h.
    Basis: external (direct) radiation only; internal dose is not part of this
    hourly test — it is captured by the annual TEDE limit in (A).

Both limits must be met simultaneously and continuously. Neither supersedes the
other, and compliance with one is not evidence of compliance with the other.

=====================================================================
2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (controlling language)
=====================================================================

§ 20.1301 Dose limits for individual members of the public.

(a) Each licensee shall conduct operations so that—

(1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from
the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of
the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration
the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered
radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in
medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive
material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and

(2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the
dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released
in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any
one hour.

(b) If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled
areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those
individuals.

(c) Notwithstanding paragraph (a)(1), a licensee may permit visitors to an
individual who cannot be released under § 35.75 to receive a radiation dose
greater than 0.1 rem (1 mSv) if (1) the dose does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv),
and (2) the authorized user has determined before the visit that it is
appropriate.

(d) A licensee or license applicant may apply for prior NRC authorization to
operate up to an annual dose limit for an individual member of the public of
0.5 rem (5 mSv), with a demonstration of need, a program to assess and control
dose within that limit, and ALARA procedures.

(e) A licensee subject to EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation
standards in 40 CFR part 190 shall also comply with those standards.

(f) The Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in
unrestricted areas and on total radionuclide quantities released in effluents to
restrict collective dose.

=====================================================================
3. DEFINITIONS THAT GOVERN HOW THE NUMBERS ARE APPLIED
=====================================================================

- 'Individual members of the public': persons who are not occupationally
  exposed by the licensee. Includes visitors, neighbors, and any member of the
  public the licensee permits into a controlled area — paragraph (b) makes clear
  the public limits still apply to them.
- 'Unrestricted area': any area to which access is not controlled by the
  licensee for purposes of protection from radiation exposure (10 CFR 20.1003).
  The hourly limit is evaluated at the boundary of / within that area, at the
  location occupied or occupiable by a member of the public.
- 'Total effective dose equivalent' (TEDE): the sum of the deep-dose equivalent
  from external exposure and the committed effective dose equivalent from
  intakes (10 CFR 20.1003).
- 'In a year': the annual limit is a 12-consecutive-month quantity, not a
  calendar-year accounting convention imposed by the rule; licensees typically
  demonstrate it over a calendar year or a defined 12-month period.
- The hourly limit has no averaging window stated in the rule. It is a
  not-to-exceed value for any one hour; a licensee may not average a short
  excursion over a longer period to show compliance with (a)(2).

=====================================================================
4. EXCLUSIONS — WHAT DOES NOT COUNT AGAINST THE LIMITS
=====================================================================

Against the ANNUAL limit (a)(1), exclude:
  1. Background radiation.
  2. Medical administration the individual has received.
  3. Exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released
     under § 35.75 (i.e., released patients).
  4. Voluntary participation in medical research programs.
  5. The licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage
     under § 20.2003.

Against the HOURLY limit (a)(2), exclude:
  1. Dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and
     released under § 35.75.

Note the asymmetry: the sewerage-disposal exclusion and the medical-research
exclusion appear only in (a)(1). Do not carry them across to the hourly test.

=====================================================================
5. HOW COMPLIANCE IS DEMONSTRATED — 10 CFR 20.1302
=====================================================================

(a) The licensee must survey radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled
    areas and radioactive materials in effluents to demonstrate compliance with
    § 20.1301.

(b) Two compliant pathways for the ANNUAL limit:

    Pathway 1 — dose-based [20.1302(b)(1)]: demonstrate by measurement or
    calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the HIGHEST
    dose from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year.
    This is a maximally-exposed-individual test, not an average-population test.

    Pathway 2 — concentration-based [20.1302(b)(2)]: demonstrate that
      (i) annual average concentrations of radioactive material in gaseous and
          liquid effluents at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed the
          values in Table 2 of Appendix B to Part 20; AND
      (ii) if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area,
          the dose from external sources would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv)
          in an hour AND 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year.

IMPORTANT — the 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) per year figure in 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) is NOT
a second or alternative public dose limit. It is a screening surrogate for the
external-source component used only when the licensee elects the
concentration-based pathway. The legally binding annual limit remains 0.1 rem
(1 mSv) TEDE under 20.1301(a)(1). A licensee that fails the 0.05 rem/yr external
screen but passes a full TEDE calculation at or below 0.1 rem/yr is compliant
with 20.1301(a)(1); it simply cannot use Pathway 2 to show it.

=====================================================================
6. UNIT CONVERSION TABLE (all values as stated in the rule)
=====================================================================

Quantity                     rem / mrem            SI (mSv / uSv)     Notes
---------------------------- --------------------- ------------------ ------------
Annual public limit (TEDE)   0.1 rem = 100 mrem    1 mSv = 1000 uSv   20.1301(a)(1)
Hourly external limit        0.002 rem = 2 mrem    0.02 mSv = 20 uSv  20.1301(a)(2)
Continuous-presence screen   0.05 rem = 50 mrem    0.5 mSv            20.1302(b)(2)(ii)
Visitor dose ceiling         0.5 rem = 500 mrem    5 mSv              20.1301(c)
Alternate annual limit (by   0.5 rem = 500 mrem    5 mSv              20.1301(d), NRC
  prior NRC authorization)                                            approval required

Conversion factors used: 1 rem = 10 mSv = 1000 mrem; 1 mSv = 100 mrem.

=====================================================================
7. THE TRAP THE TWO LIMITS SET — WHY BOTH MUST BE CHECKED
=====================================================================

2 mrem/h sustained for a full year is 2 x 8760 = 17,520 mrem = 17.52 rem, i.e.
175 times the 0.1 rem/yr limit. The hourly limit therefore does NOT authorize a
steady 2 mrem/h field in an unrestricted area. It bounds short-term peaks; the
annual limit bounds the integrated dose. Conversely, a field well under 2 mrem/h
can still blow the annual limit if occupancy is high: 0.05 rem/yr corresponds to
an average of 0.05/8760 = 5.7 urem/h (0.057 uSv/h) under continuous occupancy.

Worked check (illustrative):
  Measured field at the unrestricted-area boundary, worst-case location:
    1.5 mrem/h (0.015 mSv/h) from external sources.
  Hourly test: 1.5 mrem/h < 2 mrem/h  -> PASSES 20.1301(a)(2).
  Annual test: if continuously occupied, 1.5 mrem/h x 8760 h = 13,140 mrem
    = 13.14 rem >> 0.1 rem -> FAILS 20.1301(a)(1) unless occupancy is
    controlled/limited (e.g., fence, locked gate, posted restriction, terrain)
    such that the maximally exposed individual's annual TEDE <= 0.1 rem.
  Corrective action: reduce source term/shielding, or establish access control
  so the area is no longer unrestricted, or demonstrate by occupancy factor
  that annual TEDE <= 100 mrem including any internal contribution.

=====================================================================
8. SCOPE NOTES — WHAT THESE LIMITS DO AND DO NOT COVER
=====================================================================

- These are the NRC's general public dose limits for NRC licensees under
  10 CFR Part 20. They apply across license types (byproduct, source, special
  nuclear material) unless a specific part imposes something more restrictive.
- Facility-specific overlays that sit ON TOP of Part 20 and are not substitutes
  for it:
    * 40 CFR Part 190 (EPA environmental radiation standards for nuclear fuel
      cycle facilities): 25 mrem/yr whole body, incorporated by 20.1301(e).
    * 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I: design objectives for light-water reactors
      (e.g., 5 mrem/yr whole body from liquid effluents, 15 mrem/yr from
      gaseous effluents) — design objectives, more restrictive than Part 20,
      but not the general public limit.
    * 10 CFR Part 35 patient-release provisions, which the exclusions in
      20.1301(a) cross-reference.
    * 10 CFR Part 37 (category 1 quantities) imposes security, not public dose
      limits.
- Agreement States adopt compatible regulations; the numerical limits are
  almost universally identical to Part 20, but the citation is the State
  regulation, not 10 CFR 20.1301. Confirm the State rule if the licensee is
  Agreement State-licensed.
- DOE facilities are not NRC-licensed and fall under DOE Order 458.1 / 10 CFR
  Part 835, not Part 20.
- Occupational limits (10 CFR 20.1201) are separate and do not apply to members
  of the public.

=====================================================================
9. ONE-LINE ANSWER
=====================================================================

Annual: 0.1 rem (1 mSv) total effective dose equivalent per year to the
maximally exposed member of the public, excluding background, the individual's
medical exposure, released patients, voluntary medical research, and sewerage
disposal — 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1).
Any one hour: 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) from external sources in any unrestricted
area — 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2).
